BOR: Canada, between the blocs → split by the war
EAS: From the Pact split → Eurasian Ascendancy
USA: US Navy → United States of the Americas
UNL: United Nations of Earth and Luna
BKG: Not a conflict, but it mattered

frames.c: Mechanics check a wing hinge on an HX-4 Merlin in a coastal hangar at sunset, its tethered LR-1 rifle cradled beside it and still cabled to the capacitor pack. Only a dozen Merlins were built, and they proved a frame could fold into flight.

vehicles.c: An M9 Teamster stands watch at an alpine road tunnel in a midnight snowstorm while a truck and two tracked supply carriers file past its knees. More Teamsters serve than any other US frame, and the vehicles still do the hauling.

supers.c: A CX-1 Concord rides a heavy-lift pontoon through a canal lock in predawn rain, chained down with its weapons stowed. The 17 m escort frame on the dock reaches less than halfway up it. A dozen exist, and each one was built to be seen.

carriers.c: An AWX-1 Marlinspike drifts on a safety tether above the lunar far side, solar wings out, beside the warship whose catapult it was built for. It has no legs, and nobody yet knows how it should fight. By 2327 every carrier launches its descendants.

orgs.c: A house Rigger anchors to the torn truss of an abandoned station past the elevator and lifts out a greenhouse module that is still growing. Its two operators live in the doubled cab for a week at a time. The prospecting houses keep their own books, and claims like this one are what they settle by tether duel.

headline.c: Dawn at a dry river crossing in 2186. A sand-worn League industrial frame rests beside its supply carriers while crews and civilians get ready to move. Across the river a Kestrel waits by its battery pit, and the city behind them is burning.

fb1.c: An M4 Garrison crouches in a foothill motor pool, its M30 pointed at the ground and its pile bunker folded. From behind, the tank it grew out of is plain to see: the sloped glacis, the cupola head, the turbine louvres.

fh3.c: A Kestrel has just landed on a closed highway in the morning haze, knees still bent and dust settling. It carries its LR-3 and two missiles under each wing binder. The fans make no flame and no smoke.

xc1.c: Three Concords loom over a press stand on an airbase apron at dusk, more than twice the height of the frames parked beside them. The pilot pair stand on the chest walkway. It was meant to look like a triumph.

wS1.c: Four Garrisons ambush a tank column from a Zagros ravine in 2162. The lead frame fires a shoulder missile uphill. The tanks can't climb to where they stand.

wS7.c: At night on the Malan Bridge, the Choir kneels across the approach and holds one forearm over the crossing to catch shrapnel. Buses, handcarts and families keep moving beneath it. Its rifle stays slung.

wO1.c: Striking workers hold a pressure bulkhead aboard an orbital construction station in 2166. A four-armed AW-3 Lifter braces the structure with its upper arms and holds a rivet driver and a welding torch in its lower pair. Security waits beyond a sealed door.

c2.c: An armourer opens the stock of an LR-3 in a forward workshop to service the MHI capacitor inside. No tether runs to a power pack. Through the hangar door, a Kestrel's leg gives the rifle its scale.

q2.c: Night rain in a highway pit. An Osprey's crane arm lowers a fresh QX pack into the spine of a kneeling Kestrel, guided by crew on the catwalks. The whole swap takes about a minute and a half.

o14.c: A Pavise leads from a foggy ridge with its antenna panels open and its coilgun braced on a bipod. Two Hauberts follow it through the valley. Below, the enemy's headlights wander. You can't see the jamming, only what it does.

va22.c: Three Kafilas, turretless tank hulls packed with fuel drums, spares and shade cloth, halt at a desert rest stop at blue hour. Mechanics check tracks while a family takes on water. A Haboob stands guard far behind.

vc21.c: A Heron carries four QX packs on one sling pallet up an Afghan valley toward a forward pit, where an Osprey and a kneeling Kestrel wait.

yg22.c: A Safina, once a bucket-wheel mining crawler, rolls ahead of a sandstorm with its hangar doors open on a row of Haboobs. One frame walks down the ramp. The deck carries workshops, water treatment and a small refinery.

yh30.c: The only Rookery holds station over a cloud deck at dawn on its four ducted fans, well away from any fighting. A Harrier is secured on the service deck beside a crane and a battery pack.

sfe0.c: An armed station tug escorts a civilian tender past a construction ring in 2186. Its weapons are a rivet gun and a cutting rig bolted to its truss. A tethered worker on the hull gives the scale.

og_mhi.c: In Mitsurugi's coastal works, technicians hand-calibrate an unarmed Kizuna's fingers from a gantry. In the next bay, the capacitors that Mitsurugi sells abroad roll past on carts.

ac05.c: Gloria Abernathy defends her swap pit near Shindand during the Hari River Offensive. Her Osprey's crane arm keeps a pack steady in its socket while the other hand aims an M30 over the berm. Her crew shelter in the revetments beside a kneeling Kestrel.

QAC.c: Delegates, engineers and repair crews argue around a plain table in a shaded Khartoum courtyard in 2186. Outside, the depot keeps working: a League frame, Kafila carriers and the water queue.

UNEL.c: Projected. A lunar yard turned relief port after the war. Suited crews pass medical and rebuilding cargo through pressure locks while people inside watch a convoy leave for Earth.

wS5.c: The Great Sand Sea at dusk in 2183. Three sets of supply tracks meet at a wrecked depot among burnt-out hulls, and one Sirocco still works there. The Jinn is nowhere in sight.

fn1.c: An NK-12 stands knee-deep at an Indian field station in monsoon rain. Engineers check the cooling plumbing behind its big radiator grilles and rubber joint boots. Nashik rebuilt that cooling system twice before Moscow agreed it needed rebuilding.

fg3.c: During an evacuation drill outside Tunis, an Elissa kneels behind its rescue shield. Medics load a stretcher into one of the four pods racked behind its hips.

ac26.c: Hawa Abdelrahman's Sirocco faces the Jinn in the Great Sand Sea, the second time they meet. The Jinn stands more than twice its height. This time she lowers her gun.

xb1.c: In a cold Canadian hangar, the Aurora's upper half hangs on crane slings above its legs, two metres short of the waist ring. Calgary built the legs and Montreal the torso. When Canada splits, the halves end up on opposite sides of the line.

yg51.c: Projected. Inside a Hospital Safina well behind the North African Front, the old mech bays hold quiet wards. Behind a screen, the graft vats work.

yh51.c: Projected. The Hakobune rises on its fans over a storm-damaged Japanese coast. Two Kizunas wait in its open rescue hangar. It carries no weapons.

og_tng.h: Everyone eats at the same table
og_tng.c: Projected. The Tangier collective shares one long meal in the shipbreaking yard, mechanics and volunteers together. The half-built Tramuntana stands behind them, its curved hull ribs already part of its body.

xq1.c: Projected. The Tramuntana stands guard on a Tangier quay while families board the ferries across the strait.

wO8.h: Survey camp, according to the manifest
wO8.c: Melas Chasma, 2186. A small Ascension camp digs a careful trench at the old Specimen site, dwarfed by the canyon wall. On paper it is a survey.

xl1.c: At the south-pole yard, the crews build their own Custodian on a slipway between two half-finished ships from different blocs. Its armour is patched from all of them, every insignia ground off.

frames.label: Frames
frames.intro: Frames bring the other three trees together. Each card shows the power plant a frame runs on and the weapons it carries. Select one to see the doctrine it was built for, and follow any of those links into the other trees.
turns: Brannock's M4 was licensed by Halcyon and VEK and rebuilt by League workshops. Nearly every Western frame family traces back to it.
Two answers to the same problem
Halcyon put wings on a licensed ground frame and bet on speed. Tianlong went the other way: simpler, heavier and built in thousands.
Turbine vents on Brannock backs, big diesel torsos on Tianlong, battery spines on Kestrels, fuel-cell stacks behind VEK hardpoints. You can tell a bloc by its outline.

Mitsurugi's PT-X Raijin is the first frame designed around an energy weapon. Every bloc wants it, and Japan can't sell it without picking a side. Mitsurugi has started registering subsidiaries abroad, just in case.

Boreal in Canada, Nashik in India and the Tunis Works on the Maghreb coast all started on someone else's licence, in places their patrons don't fully control. All three are already designing for whatever comes after.
fams: Tanks with legs, built to be fixed with a wrench.
Modular knights, and hand-built frames for aces.
Cold-weather frames from a country that buys from both blocs.
Iron mountains, in their thousands, and lately the network that moves them.
Heavy, aggressive, and few. Built in Russia, and now in India.
OKB-7's Indian line, learning to build frames for sworn pilots.
Rescuers first, then the world's best actuators.
Three blocs' parts on one frame, until Khartoum starts designing its own.
French and Italian engineering on the Maghreb coast, and the Charter's second design office.

nodes.x: Halcyon's fighter and ground-attack jets. The wing binders, avionics and flight-control software of every Halcyon frame descend from them.
The first mech that could fold into a flight mode. Transformation took eleven seconds, and the tethered LR-1 had to be stowed first. Only a dozen were built, but they proved the idea.

nodes.t: Licensed Garrison, lightened for air drops
nodes.x: Halcyon's first mech was a licensed Brannock M4 Garrison with its armour cut back so a tiltrotor could carry it. The Army never forgave Halcyon for improving its design.

The Merlin's flight mode on the Sparrowhawk's ground frame. Two-second transformation, a quick-swap battery spine driving electric ducted fans in the calf nacelles, and an LR-3 in hand. Its forty-minute endurance defined US doctrine.

nodes.t: Heavier strike Kestrel with point defence
nodes.x: A bigger Kestrel with QX-3 packs, more wing stores, and a PL-2 laser to survive the Pact's anti-air rockets and the Sapsans' missiles. Slightly slower to transform, much harder to shoot down. Svalbard turned it from an option into the standard.

nodes.t: Swap-pit support frame with battery crane
nodes.x: A non-transforming frame on the Sparrowhawk line, built to run swap pits: a battery crane on one arm, an M30 on the other, and Brannock hybrid power for endurance. Pit crews fight in them when the pit is attacked, which is often.

nodes.t: Harrier with a microwave power receiver
nodes.x: A Harrier with a dorsal rectenna for the SKYLINE beamed-power trials. Two exist. One has flown for six hours without landing.
Brannock-Hale's tank business supplied the armour layout, fire control and crew-survival thinking for every frame it builds.
Hydraulic legged rigs for demolition and logging on steep ground. The first machines to walk at this scale.

nodes.t: The first mech in combat service
nodes.x: A construction walker's legs under a tank's armour and fire control. Slow, loud and very hard to kill. It's been licensed, copied or rebuilt by almost everyone.

nodes.t: Heavy frame that holds swap points
nodes.x: Extra armour and a second Hornet pod, built to seize and hold the swap points Kestrels depend on. The Army calls it the frame that keeps the Air Force flying, and says so often.
The Garrison redesigned for fire teams: hybrid power that lets it go quiet in ambush, standard Hornet mounts, and a stake driver on the left arm. More Teamsters serve than any other US frame.
A Teamster rebuilt around a frame-sized HT-20 plant and the AR-40E electrothermal rifle: the Army's attempt to match linear-weapon penetration without depending on Halcyon.
European wheeled reconnaissance vehicles, whose sensor masts and quiet running shaped VEK's priorities.
A licence-built M4 Garrison with a VEK sensor head and a submarine-derived fuel cell in place of the turbine. Quieter and sharper-eyed than the original, and the first mono-eye frame.
VEK's first clean-sheet design, built around the standard hardpoint and BZ-4 stacks. Rounded knightly armour, a mono-eye on a track, and one frame reconfigured overnight for any role.

nodes.t: Lance knight of the hunter-killer lance
nodes.x: A heavier Haubert built to close and finish: reinforced arms for the HEAT lance, a large shield, and BZ-6 reformer stacks so it can refuel from any truck.
Carries the Spiegel coilgun, the Union's best EW suite and Fenrir missiles. It leads formations under Directive 5 and takes the kill shot under Directive 8.

nodes.t: Hand-built ace frame on Haubert bones
nodes.x: Castellani's take on the Haubert: lighter armour, Stack-R racing cells and hand-tuned actuators. Each one is built for one named ace and painted red and gold.

nodes.t: Plasma-blade prototype for the top ace
nodes.x: Built around the Lama Ardente plasma blade, with Destrier-style arm bracing and a licensed capacitor core in the chest. It fights at full power for about forty seconds.
Tracked haulers and snow tractors that kept northern mines supplied across winter ice roads. Boreal's heated drivetrains, and its habit of wasting no heat at all, start here.

Canada's first frames were Brannock M4 Garrisons built under licence in Calgary, with heated actuators, wide snowshoe feet and a turbine that would start at forty below. Washington set the licence terms; Ottawa paid them.

nodes.t: Arctic frame on US bones with a Union sensor head
nodes.x: Boreal's first own design: a Teamster-pattern chassis on snowshoe feet, a hybrid plant that can idle for a week on one tank of diesel, and a VEK sensor head, bought because Washington wouldn't export its newest one. US officers call it a Teamster for people who don't trust the US Army. Norway bought forty.

nodes.t: Runs as cold as the ice it hides in
nodes.x: Built after Svalbard, where the Union showed that whoever is seen first loses. The Wolverine can lie in the snow for days on a reformer-stack trickle, with an insulated hull and passive sensors, and its thermal signature is close to the ice around it. Its fuel cells are Union-pattern. So, increasingly, are its customers.

nodes.t: Sealed long-endurance frame for the high Arctic
nodes.x: Officially a search-and-rescue frame: a sealed cab two people can live in for a month, a heat-recovery loop that wastes almost nothing, and a power budget counted in watts rather than kilowatts. Boreal builds it in Calgary and Montreal, either side of a line nobody has drawn yet. The Halifax Motion passed the week it was unveiled, and Ottawa and Washington have argued about who owns it ever since. Its life-support loop will outlast the country that built it.
Tianlong's civilian excavators and tractors supplied the diesel-electric drive, the hydraulics and the factories.
An excavator drive train in an egg-shaped armoured torso, with a tank gun on the shoulder that could only fire from a kneel. Thousands were built, and many still serve in the League.

nodes.t: “Iron Mountain”: the most-built mech in the world
nodes.x: Adopted the same year as the Type-09 cannon it was built to carry. Thick armour, few moving parts, a cockpit buried deep in the torso, and a multi-fuel diesel. Six weeks to train a pilot.

nodes.t: Depot upgrade: radios, optics, drum rifle
nodes.x: Tieshans upgraded at depot level with better radios, optics and Type-07 drum rifles, so older frames can be brought up to standard without new production lines. The new radios carry Tianshu's data link, which is the real upgrade.
A squat, heavily armoured Tieshan derivative built to be dug in, with a Type-09 cannon and anti-air rocket racks for the Air Umbrella. It barely walks and never retreats.

nodes.t: “Sky Eye”: one pilot, a Tianshu node, six uncrewed frames
nodes.x: Beijing's answer to augmented pilots: change the network, not the pilot. A Tieshan-Kai chassis with a Tianshu node in the torso, an unaugmented pilot, and command of six uncrewed Tieshan conversions that walk wherever Tianshu sends them. The network proposes and the pilot approves. In trials the uncrewed frames hold a kneeling line better than conscripts do. Nobody has yet tested what happens when the link is jammed.

OKB-7 enlarged the Tieshan chassis, fitted twin diesels, built a rotary cannon into each forearm and added a Grad-M battery. The Pact's first frame built for quality over numbers. Since the Delhi Accession, a second OKB-7 line at Nashik builds them too.
The breakthrough frame: a Molot autoloader, a Grad-M battery and armour that shrugs off rifle fire. It opens the gap the waves behind it pour through.

nodes.t: Elite rail frame for augmented pilots
nodes.x: A lighter, faster Medved derivative with a Type-12 rail rifle and a KN-1 capacitor. Its control system assumes an augmented pilot; ordinary pilots black out in it. Beijing has never fielded one.
The heaviest conventional frame ever built. It anchors itself with spades and fires the Kalibr-305, or carries the Iskra particle cannon fed by cable from an MTU-7 truck.
A Mamont chassis carrying the Pamir micro-reactor. It can run for weeks. Its pilots' radiation exposure is a state secret.
Decades of Indian factories building foreign fighters and tanks under licence, and learning more from each contract than the licensor meant to teach.

nodes.t: OKB-7's heavy frame, rebuilt for heat and monsoon
nodes.x: The price of the Delhi Accession: Medveds built at Nashik under OKB-7 supervision, with sealed joints for the monsoon, larger radiators for the plains, and Indian crews for the breakthrough groups. Nashik's engineers rebuilt the cooling system twice before Moscow agreed it needed rebuilding.

Nashik's first clean-sheet design, built around the Nashik Oath rather than Department Zero: two lighter, Volk-derived frames that fight as a sworn pair, linked so that each pilot sees what the other sees. The augmentation is worn, not implanted: a pilot rig that comes off and goes back to the unit store. The Ashvins are the twin divine horsemen of the old stories. Moscow wants the pair for the breakthrough groups; their pilots want them for the line.
Decades of Japanese work on rescue robots and powered exoskeletons, the origin of Mitsurugi's lead in actuators and balance control.
An unarmed rescue frame for earthquakes and tsunamis, with the best balance control and hands in the world. The Japanese public met mechs as rescuers first.
A clean humanoid frame for coast and island defence, with hybrid cells, a Type-L coil carbine and an HF-1 sonic blade. Understated outside, superb actuators inside.

nodes.t: Upgraded Hayate for live test units
nodes.x: A Hayate with spare power and mounts for whatever prototype the lab sends next. The live test units fly them.

nodes.t: First frame built around a beam weapon
nodes.x: A Shiden rebuilt around one weapon, and lopsided because of it: a braced right shoulder and forearm cradle for the BX-0 emitter, and a cooling module on the left of the back with thermal cartridges the ground crew swap between test strings. It's the first frame designed around an energy weapon rather than adapted to carry one, with a Mk.III core behind the right chest. Clean white with blue and red accents, and no crest. One exists, and every bloc's intelligence service knows where it is kept.
Surplus M4 Garrisons and Type-01 Tieniu rebuilt in League workshops with sand filters and whatever parts were available. Every League frame starts here.
Qadira's first production frame: a licensed Tieniu torso on Garrison-pattern legs with wide desert feet. Ugly and reliable, and the League has stuck with that approach since.
The current League frame: a Q-Mix turbine, second-hand VEK sensor heads, and mounts that take US or Eurasian pods. Every part has a supplier in at least two blocs.

nodes.t: Kestrel airframe, VEK sensors, MHI blade
nodes.x: Grey Lantern builds from bought and stolen parts: a Kestrel airframe with the transformation removed, a VEK sensor head, an MHI sonic blade. No two are alike, and none are legal.

nodes.t: Built in Khartoum to hold ground and shelter people
nodes.x: The first Qadira frame designed in Khartoum instead of assembled from three blocs' parts: a Sirocco chassis with a sealed cab, a dozer-blade shield wide enough to cover a family, a water tank and field medical bay in the hull, and a Q-Mix turbine re-tuned for local fuels. Its designers spent a month in the Great Sand Sea watching how the Jinn moves among people. It is the line the League will keep building after it stops being a league.

Shipyards in Tunis and Bizerte and rail works in Algiers that built ferries, rolling stock and tractors under French and Italian licence for most of a century. Their engineers learned the European way of doing things, and kept the old Carthaginian habit of trading with everyone.

nodes.t: Haubert built in Tunis for the Union's partners
nodes.x: After the Maghreb Depot Strikes, Strasbourg promised its North African partners they would never again be left blind or stranded, and opened a Haubert line in Tunis to prove it: sealed joints, sand filters, a dust-shielded mono-eye track and a finish of sand and slate. French engineers ran the plant. Tunisian and Algerian crews built and flew the frames, and named them after the wind from the north.

Castellani opened a workshop beside the Tunis line to build Falcos for the partner states' aces, then a cheaper frame for the rest of their lances: Falco-pattern actuators, BZ-6 stacks that refuel from any truck, and a tall sensor mast for the open desert. Its Tunisian pilots gave it the Italian name for the hot wind off the Sahara. The Italian engineers who came for three years have stayed for ten.

nodes.t: The Charter's first frame from Tunis
nodes.x: When the Maghreb signed the Khartoum Charter, the Tunis works went with it, and so did most of the French and Italian engineers who ran them. Under Qadira they are building a frame that keeps the Union's standard hardpoints and Castellani's hand-tuned joints on a chassis built for Protect First: a shield arm, an evacuation cradle on the back, and room in the cab for a medic. It is named after Carthage's founding queen. Strasbourg has asked for its licences back. Tunis has not replied.
One-person pods with manipulator arms that built the first stations.
Four arms, vestigial legs used as anchors, and a big thruster pack. The standard station worker frame, and the one the workers armed in the labour dispute.
A bigger worker frame with solar-fuel power for multi-day shifts and a tether harpoon for salvage. Safety yellow with hazard stripes.
Officially a station-security variant. In practice, a Rigger with armour plates, an RD-12 spike driver and a boarding harpoon. Every bloc has bought some.

Built for the catapults of the first warships, with no legs and a Halcyon linear rifle in place of construction tools. Nobody yet knows how it should fight. In the war its descendants learn, and by 2327 every carrier launches them beside fighter craft.

supers.label: Supers
supers.intro: Super robots appear late in Gen 2. Each one is a different answer to the same question: what can the human spirit be made to do? Some programs harness it, some encourage it, some abuse it. Only the Martian line comes from the Specimen. The rest are human work: heretical science, latent spirit, or technology pushed further than it should go.
turns: Ascension's Ares mission brought back more than rocks. Outside Station Nine, almost nobody knows.
A leash made of a person
H-17, Halden's first growth, only went still once a human mind bonded with it. Every Halden pilot since has been chosen to be a leash.
A year ago the United States unveiled the Concord class as a deterrent. Every hidden program in the world sped up overnight.
Thirteen ways to use a soul

Leashed, befriended, consumed, shared, disciplined, preserved, replaced, knighted, divided, hired, escaped, sworn to all, hunted in packs. Five answer to no government. Each is a first draft of a philosophy that will outlive Earth, though not always the one its authors meant.

In Tangier, a workshop collective builds a giant from the North African Front's wreckage and elects its crew. When the war ends, the Commonwealth asks it to serve, and it is the only super that ever agreed to.
fams: One alien source, treated two opposite ways.
Heretical science. The pilot becomes the control system.
Technology pushed too far, and made to work. The first super built in series, from a company Congress chartered.
Change the network, not the pilot.
Latent spirit and a fusion reactor. Nobody agrees which one is doing the work.
A knight for a union that put its giants on trial.
A country between the blocs, built in two halves.
Built by crews sworn to every bloc, and so to none.
Scrap, volunteers, and a crew that votes.
Heretical science outside any bloc. The dead, still choosing.

nodes.t: Dormant giant body from Valles Marineris
nodes.x: A giant humanoid body, partly mineralised, neither clearly alive nor dead. Its tissue responds to human presence: monitors show activity when people are near, and more when they are afraid, angry or grieving. Nobody knows what it is or who made it.

Launched by Ascension from the orbital elevator about thirty years ago. Officially a geology mission whose crew came home to a parade. The mission log has a forty-hour gap, and two of the four crew never gave another interview. In 2186, one of those two led the settlers who founded Colony One.
A sealed station in high orbit, built during Gen 1 to hold the Specimen: too dangerous to bring down to Earth, too valuable to abandon. Most Ascension staff believe Station Nine is a fuel depot.

nodes.t: Growing giant tissue from Martian samples
nodes.x: The Halden Institute bought tissue samples from Station Nine, or stole them; even Halden isn't sure which. Its Geneva laboratories spent a decade learning to grow the tissue into structure. Each culture gets an accession number; most never grow past a sample.

The first culture accession to mature to full size. Accession numbers count cultures, not giants: the sixteen before it died as samples. On activation it killed two technicians, then went still the moment its first pilot, in a test cab bolted to the laboratory rig, came online through the contact interfaces. The restraint frame was built around it in the weeks afterwards. H-17 was lost in a League proxy war three years ago.

Two separately grown organisms in the same pattern of restraint frame: a load-bearing exoframe with joint brakes, armour panels and an armoured operator cab in the chest. Each is bonded to a pilot Halden chose for psychological profile rather than skill, and is calm only while that pilot is connected through the cab. The tissue moves itself. The bundle from the grid carries perfusion, cooling and the suppression cycle, and off the bundle a giant lasts as long as its heat and metabolite load allow: minutes in a hard fight. H-31 matures faster than H-24 and needs nearly twice the cooling. Halden treats pilots as a replaceable part of the restraint system, and has already replaced one.

nodes.t: In the tank, and it has chosen a pilot
nodes.x: Still growing in Geneva under a laboratory accession, never commissioned. At night, with the suppression cycle at full strength, its monitors record coordinated movement. Suppression is supposed to make that impossible. Last month it went still for the first time, on the night a laboratory cleaner's fourteen-year-old daughter waited out a shift in the observation gallery. It is calm whenever she is in the building and restless whenever she isn't. Halden's scientists have told the ethics panel. They have not told her.

H-17, after its restraint frame shattered and its pilot died in a League proxy war. A League mechanic found it in the sand and saw what Halden never had: the suppression cycle was causing the distress Halden treated as aggression. With the cycle cut, it stopped fighting. The mechanic rebuilt the wrecked cab around a scavenged Sirocco cockpit and pilots it from inside the chest. With no grid bundle it lives on what the League brings it: water, feedstock and rest, delivered by Kafila carriers. It carries a Type-01Q cannon like a pistol. Every bloc wants it recovered or destroyed. Its pilot wants to help people.

nodes.t: Study the Specimen where it was found
nodes.x: Under the ethics panel's review, Halden's surviving scientists have proposed the only program the panel might approve: a sealed, supervised station in Valles Marineris, run on evidence, where nothing is grown or altered that can't be justified as necessary. The panel's conditions run to four hundred pages. They are the first draft of how the Union would govern Mars.

nodes.t: Khartoum learns to heal the Jinn
nodes.x: The people who keep the Jinn alive have learned to culture its tissue to patch its wounds, and found that the grafts adapt to whatever body they are given. Khartoum's medical council has started trials on burn victims. The keepers' rule is that the Jinn is cared for, not commanded. Not everyone in the League sees a medicine. The raid cadres who never accepted Protect First see soldiers who don't die.

nodes.t: Direct brain control of small frames
nodes.x: Before the capsule, Department Zero tested direct neural control on small frames, using volunteers who were not always volunteers.

The pilot is sealed in a fluid capsule and their nervous system becomes the control system. With no body to protect, the frame is built far past normal limits. A cable-fed reactor carriage follows it on tracks. Every sortie does cumulative damage to the pilot's nervous system. Officials set a nominal sortie allowance, and few pilots reach it. The name means the Deathless, because the machine outlives every pilot.

nodes.t: Designed for a pilot who never leaves
nodes.x: The second Koschei has a rear service assembly for installing the pilot and running life support, and no emergency extraction at all. Department Zero calls this an engineering simplification. Its first pilot was installed in the spring. In the third week the interface began returning the same three words on every channel, in the pilot's own phrasing: let me out. Department Zero has classified it as signal noise. The engineers who wrote the interface have stopped coming to the trials.

The Indian pilots augmented for the breakthrough groups refused transfer to Department Zero and wrote an oath instead. Enhancement is equipment, issued for a duty and owed back to the unit. No pilot is sealed in a capsule. The strong defend those who can't be changed. Their crews call them ashva, horses, bred and sworn for the line. Moscow hasn't decided whether it can tolerate them; Beijing pretends they don't exist.

nodes.t: Splitting neural load across two pilots
nodes.x: A US study found that two pilots on linked interfaces could run a frame far too complex for one. The test pairs also started finishing each other's sentences.

A 40 m super-heavy built from scaled-up real-robot technology: the first full-scale HT-20 plant, built years before anyone could fit one in a normal frame, an electrothermal cannon, a stake driver the size of a tree. One Army pilot and one Air Force pilot share the neural load, and it only works if they trust each other completely. A dozen exist. The scarce part is compatible pilot pairs, not hardware. It was the first super the world saw, and it was built to be seen.
A three-pilot version. In trials, the third pilot can't always tell afterwards which memories are their own.

nodes.t: A calm mind steadies the fusion loop
nodes.x: During Amaterasu trials, staff noticed the reactor ran steadier when one technician was on the console, a former shrine attendant who meditated on shift. Tsukuyomi Lab quietly began recruiting from shrines.

The Amaterasu reactor would never fit in a normal frame, so the lab built a mech big enough for the reactor. White, blue and red, with a sun-disc chest and radiator fins that glow under load. It holds stable only with a shrine-trained pilot. Engineers call it biofeedback; priests call it the kami. Fusion lets it fire a scaled-up BX-0 continuously, which the Raijin's capacitor-fed emitter can't do. It is the one weapon Japan legally cannot own.
Pilots are trained in a mountain shrine that also serves as a JSDF facility. Training takes years of discipline before the trainee ever touches the controls. Only one is ready.

nodes.t: Mind-maps sold to families in orbit
nodes.x: Vireo's shell companies have started selling mind-mapping off-world. The first buyers are the families crewing Tianlong's prospecting tenders, who record their elders so a house never loses what it knows. Nobody asked Beijing. The families treat the recordings as part of the house's capital, bargained over like any other asset.
Vireo began as a medical startup offering terminal patients a recording of their mind. For years the recordings did nothing. Then they started running.

nodes.t: Eleven pilots, recorded before they died
nodes.x: Terminally ill and fatally wounded pilots from every bloc, recorded with consent, or something like it. They argue about whether they are the pilots or copies of them.

A giant run by the mind-maps of eleven dead pilots, built from parts Vireo bought quietly from every bloc. They vote on every action, and they have chosen to intervene where no government will: evacuations, disasters, and wars that the blocs are content to let burn. No government has discovered it yet.

Beijing's answer to the Concord and to Department Zero at once: a giant built on Tieshan engineering, with a Tianshu core in the chest and one unaugmented officer in an armoured cab who approves what the network proposes. No compatible pairs, no shrine, no capsule: any graduate of the Order 21 course can sit in it. Tianlong has built four and has tooling for forty. It is named for the bird of the old story who set out to fill the sea one pebble at a time. The Concord is no longer the only super built in series. Nobody has yet asked what the officer is for while the link holds, or what the giant does when it doesn't.

The one Koschei pilot who reached the sortie allowance and kept going. On what was meant to be her last sortie she cut the range's command link, turned her frame north and walked it off the test ground with the reactor carriage tracking behind her. Department Zero lists the frame as destroyed in testing. Its pilot is still sealed in the capsule, her nerves failing more slowly than the medical staff predicted, and nobody knows whose side she is on, only whose side she is not. The range crews named her for the warrior princess who chained Koschei in the old tale. Delhi's officers keep her file open.

Castellani's answer to Halden, and the only super the ethics panel has approved: nothing grown, nothing implanted, nothing its pilot can't walk away from. A red-and-gold knight scaled up from the Saetta, with a capacitor-fed plasma blade the crews call Durendal, a tower shield, and a command horn, Olifant, that ties every lance within a hundred kilometres into one picture. Its pilot is the ace who flew the Saetta, and the panel's one condition is that the pilot may refuse any order. Strasbourg presents it as the heir of Roland and Charlemagne's paladins, and every member state's schoolchildren know the song. In the song, Roland dies because he is too proud to sound his horn. Castellani built the horn first.

A super in two halves: the lower built in Calgary, the upper in Montreal, standing as one giant only when they lock together. Each half carries one pilot, and the pair share the neural load on an interface Boreal licensed from the Twin-Pilot Load Study, which Canada's share of the defence fund helped pay for. The two pilots have trained together for six years, one from each side of a line nobody has drawn yet. Boreal meant it as the picture of a country that holds together. When Canada splits, the halves end up on opposite sides of the Manitoba–Ontario line, and so do the pilots.

The lunar yard builds warships for every bloc and swears its crews to none, and the Custodian is what the crews are building for themselves: a giant raised in the slipway between contracts from every bloc's hull offcuts, Marlinspike catapult gear and a Halcyon linear core, powered off the ring. Ascension's books list it as a yard tug. It carries no bloc's markings, because it carries pieces of all of them. When the yards close the lanes to Earth, it is what the crews stand in front of, and UNEL's Luna bastion is named for it.

Grey Lantern's super, assembled from Concord parts that left Joint Heavy Systems' depots on paperwork nobody can trace: a salvaged HT-20 plant, one and a half sets of limbs, and a cab rebuilt for whoever is paying. The twin-pilot interface only works for a pair who trust each other completely, so Grey Lantern pairs strangers on contract and sedates away the difference. It has never fought the same way twice and has never been quite right. It is for hire by the week, and the container ship that carried it through the Panama Canal is why Panama now opens every container.

Moscow's answer to giants it can't match in the open: six Volks rebuilt by OKB-7 as a hunting pack, with lighter armour, spiked climbing feet, tether harpoons, and Type-12 rail rifles loaded with tungsten penetrators. Their links give all six pilots one picture of the quarry. The method is old: cable the legs, bring it down, go for the cab. The pilots are augmented volunteers from the breakthrough groups, the last generation Department Zero will ever train. Their first quarry is Morevna. They have found her twice and come back without her both times, and their reports have stopped calling her a target. In the war they hunt Jingweis across Central Asia, and when the Ascendancy closes Department Zero it keeps the pack, which by then swears the Nashik Oath in Russian.

Projected. In the shipbreaking yards at Tangier, a workshop collective of Moroccan mechanics and Southern Crossing volunteers, most of them Spanish and many of them Catalan, builds a giant from what the North African Front leaves behind. Its spine is a cut-down section of a scrapped Spanish dock ship's bottom hull, with keel and curved bilge ribs reshaped into its pelvis, lower back and shoulder structure, its limbs are wrecked Mistrals and Siroccos, and its heart is a bank of re-tuned Q-Mix turbines. Nobody owns it. The workshop is run by assembly, the crew is elected and paid the same as the welders, everyone eats at the same table, and the hull is painted red and black under slogans in Darija, Spanish and Catalan. Like the Charter's frames it is named for a wind: the Tramuntana, the north wind of Catalonia. It holds the Strait while the ferries cross. When the war ends, the Commonwealth asks it to serve rather than ordering it to, and the assembly votes yes.

conflicts.label: Conflicts
conflicts.intro: Thirty years of conflict, from the Ares mission in 2156 to the founding of Colony One, the first permanent settlement on another planet, and the fault lines that run from them into the Third World War. Each one explains something in the other trees: a doctrine, a weapon, a stolen design, or a super robot. The dashed column is projected: the war itself, which hasn't happened yet.
turns: At Iron Gate, four Garrisons destroyed a tank column in eleven minutes. Within a year every bloc had ordered mechs.
The theft that armed the East
The Pact lost the Battle of the Talysh Mountains but came away with LR-1 plans and a Mk.I core. Every Eastern linear weapon starts there.
The Zarqa Campaign introduced drop-and-strike. The Air Umbrella, the hunter-killer lance and the Harrier all exist because of it.
At Mong Hsat the UN destroyed a warlord every bloc had armed, because none of them could veto it without saying so. It was the first time Geneva had won anything by force, and every bloc noticed.
The Concord reveal turned super robots into a public arms race, while the two supers nobody controls are out protecting civilians.
Beijing wants Department Zero shut down; Moscow and Delhi won't allow it. On a map the Pact is still one bloc. Its own staff officers no longer think so.
fams: Where the blocs fight each other by proxy, and where a pan-African bloc takes shape.
The Pact's borders, the wars along them, and the line it will break along.
Two Western blocs that are allies on paper, and the hemisphere Washington considers its own.
Japan's quiet front line, the factories everyone wants, and the islands to the south.
Where nobody has fought a real war yet.

nodes.t: Future League states refuse bloc membership
nodes.x: Resource states across the Middle East, Africa and South Asia jointly refused to join any bloc. It made them neutral on paper and a battleground in practice.

nodes.t: United States vs insurgent armour in the Zagros foothills
nodes.x: The first mech combat. Four Brannock-Hale M4 Garrisons with M30s and ATGM tubes ambushed a tank column from a ravine the tanks couldn't climb, and destroyed it in eleven minutes. Within a year every bloc had ordered mechs.

The United States tried dropping licensed Sparrowhawks behind insurgent lines by tiltrotor. The mechs did well; the tiltrotors did not, and nine were shot down in a month. Halcyon's answer was a mech that could fly itself in.

nodes.t: United States vs a Pact-backed government
nodes.x: Officially the Zarqa Campaign, after the Jordanian city where it began. Kestrels made their combat debut with drop-and-strike, landing, fighting and leaving inside their battery limit. Pact advisers taught the defenders to hide for forty minutes and then hit the swap pits. Every bloc's doctrine since has been a reaction to this war.

nodes.t: Desert militias vs every bloc's supply lines
nodes.x: In the wreckage of the Zarqa Campaign, militias in Haboob frames raided convoys from all sides until foreign presence cost more than it was worth. A year later the African states founded the Pan-African League on armed neutrality, and the Gulf states, Pakistan and Bangladesh signed on as associates.

nodes.t: UN frames escort food through the raid zone
nodes.x: In the Convoy Raids the militias hit UN food convoys as readily as any bloc's. Geneva asked every bloc for escort frames and all three refused, so it bought Copperbelt mining walkers and Technical Refits, painted them white and crewed them with volunteers. When the blocs left, the white frames stayed. The new League let them use its roads on one condition: they never fired except to protect a convoy. They kept to it, and they were the only foreign frames it let in.

nodes.t: League factions backed by the Union, the Pact and Grey Lantern
nodes.x: A League civil war that became three proxy wars at once, fought in Siroccos and Lantern Customs. The Union secretly deployed Halden's H-17 to end it. Its restraint frame failed, its pilot died, and it vanished into the dunes. A white convoy's escort filmed it falling, and Geneva sent the footage to every parliament in the Union on the same morning. Months later, a League mechanic walked out of the desert with it. It also opened a rift that never closed: the League's Gulf associates had bankrolled the losing side.
Reports keep coming from the Great Sand Sea of a giant that stands between militias and villages, then leaves. Three blocs have sent teams to recover it. None have come back with it.

nodes.t: An unidentified giant in a city under shelling
nodes.x: During a Pact-backed bombardment of Herat, an unknown giant held the Malan Bridge over the Hari River open for nine hours while civilians crossed, then disappeared. No bloc has claimed it. It was the Choir. Geneva's resolution condemning the bombardment was vetoed by the Pact, so the Secretary-General read the names of Herat's dead into the record instead. It took four hours.

nodes.t: The League promises to fight for something
nodes.x: The League's members, joined by Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, signed a charter in Khartoum: mutual defence, shared reconstruction, and a promise to protect people before territory. The Gulf associates were invited and didn't come. Qadira moved its design office to Khartoum the same month, and took over the Union's licence plant in Tunis along with most of the French and Italian engineers who ran it. It is the first time the League has promised to fight for anything except being left alone.

nodes.t: Influence, not territory, from the Gulf to Bangladesh
nodes.x: Projected. The Gulf states, Iraq, Iran, Pakistan and Bangladesh become a frontline held by influence rather than territory: the League leans on the Gulf and Iraq, Beijing on Pakistan, Delhi on Bangladesh, and everyone fights over Iran.

Projected. The Union's old Maghreb partners are Charter states now, and every power that needs the Mediterranean wants its southern shore. The fighting runs from Morocco to the Nile. The League fights it as the African Union, and after the war it becomes the African Commonwealth.

nodes.t: The Jinn's tissue cultures go missing
nodes.x: Raiders who had fought for the League since the Convoy Raids ambushed a Kafila convoy carrying the Jinn's tissue cultures to Khartoum. Two crews died and four cultures are still missing. Khartoum says it was bandits. The keepers know the raiders' names, because until the Charter they were on the same side.

nodes.t: Healing made into a weapon, then a duty
nodes.x: Projected. The missing cultures reappear on the North African Front, inside raid battalions whose soldiers survive wounds that should kill them. As the war grinds on, the League stops arguing: grafting is how it keeps anyone alive on the worst fronts, and then simply how it keeps people. The most changed are sent furthest, to Jupiter. Umoja begins there, still using the keepers' word for it: care.

nodes.t: Europeans and Americans go south to the Charter
nodes.x: Projected. As the European Front breaks and American cities are mobilised for the war economy, people who want no part of either bloc go south: across the Mediterranean to Tunis, Algiers and Alexandria, and across the Atlantic to Dakar and Lagos. Many are French and Italian, with family ties to the old Maghreb partnership; many more are leftists with no room left in either bloc's politics. They bring languages, engineers and arguments, and the Commonwealth that comes out of the war is more plural for it.

nodes.t: Pact vs US-backed Afghan forces in the Wakhan Corridor
nodes.x: The Tieniu's combat debut. Crews fired standing, outside the cannon's safe envelope, and the recoil threw frames off their feet; by the second week they were kneeling to fire, as the manual said. The Pact also captured a dozen M30s, which became the Type-07.

nodes.t: Pact vs United States, over Azerbaijan
nodes.x: A Pact push into Azerbaijan brought the United States in. At the Battle of the Talysh Mountains, a handful of Merlins with LR-1 linear rifles destroyed a Tieniu column from beyond its range. The Pact lost the battle but won the intelligence war: within a year it had LR-1 plans and a captured Mk.I capacitor core.

nodes.t: Pact digs in; a US probe is repulsed
nodes.x: After the Caspian Crisis the Pact dug Tieshan firing lines into its borders. A US probing raid, Operation Highland, ran into one and lost a third of its frames in an afternoon. No bloc has tried to invade the Pact since.

The debut of OKB-7's breakthrough groups: Medveds and Mamonts opening gaps for Tieshan waves. Observers also saw a fast, wolf-like frame that moved in ways no ordinary pilot could survive. It was the first sighting of the Volk.

Kalibr-305 mortars, Iskra cannons and MTU-7 trucks are gathering near the border. Satellite photos show a 50 m shape lying across several oversize flatcars under tarpaulins. Every bloc is asking what war the Pact is preparing for. Some of the people asking work in Beijing.

nodes.t: India joins the Pact as a junior partner
nodes.x: India backed the Hari River Offensive with airfields and fuel, and a year later joined the Pact outright. The price was industrial: OKB-7 opened a second Medved and Mamont line at Nashik, and Indian officers joined the breakthrough groups. Beijing welcomed a third member. Delhi has voted with Moscow ever since.

nodes.t: Beijing's planning network names the second front
nodes.x: Asked to plan for a two-front war, Tianshu returned a plan in which the second front was Moscow. Beijing classified it within the hour. Within the month, someone in Moscow had read it. Beijing's position is that the network models every contingency. Moscow's is that Beijing kept asking.

nodes.t: Beijing and Moscow split over Department Zero
nodes.x: At a closed session of the Pact General Staff in Astana, Beijing's delegation demanded that Department Zero be shut down and its pilot records handed over. Moscow refused, Delhi backed Moscow, and the session ended without a communiqué. Since then the Fortress Belt and the Air Umbrella answer to Tianshu, and the breakthrough groups answer to Moscow. On paper there is still one General Staff.

nodes.t: UN white squads destroy a warlord's army in the Shan Hills
nodes.x: In 2174 a company of the export Tieshans guarding the Pact's Mekong dam went unpaid for a winter and walked into the Shan Hills with their frames. Their commander styled himself the Iron Sawbwa, after the old Shan princes. For ten years he ran jade mines and drug labs on forced labour, kept his Tieshans running on parts bought from both ends of the Pact, and shelled refugee camps across the Thai border for sheltering his deserters. After the Tianshu Forecast, Beijing would not let Delhi's forces near its border and Moscow would not let Beijing's in. When the Secretary-General put a resolution to the Security Council, the Pact could not veto it without explaining who had been selling him parts, and the United States would not defend a man flying Pact frames. It passed with every bloc abstaining. Two white squads went up the valley at Mong Hsat behind a Brazilian major in a Haubert. In two days they destroyed eleven Tieshans, and the Sawbwa died in the last of them. It was the first time UN frames had fired first. Geneva says it will be the last. Nobody who flew at Mong Hsat believes it.

nodes.t: The Pact breaks into Chinese and Russian–Indian blocs
nodes.x: Projected. The two General Staffs stop pretending. Central Asia, where both sides' railways meet, becomes the front. Mongolia and the Steppe outriders side with Beijing, and the fighting goes where they know the rail lines and Moscow's planners don't. What comes out of it is China and the Eurasian Ascendancy.

Projected. Moscow's breakthrough groups and siege trains turn west into a Continental Union whose council is still voting on how to respond. Twenty-six national contingents wait on twenty-six parliaments while the line gives way from the Baltic to the Black Sea. Behind the line, a few cities split along the old Maghreb question, street by street. What survives is refounded as the Transatlantic Union. Its institutions bind tightly enough that no single member can stop the whole from acting, and a doctrine of deliberate mixing means no city splits that way again. It is still slow, but never again paralysed.

nodes.t: Washington hands frame procurement to its makers
nodes.x: A year after Iron Gate, Congress needed mechs faster than the Pentagon could buy them. The Defense Production Partnership Act let Brannock-Hale and Halcyon design, build, crew-train and maintain their own frames, with company engineers holding reserve commissions and company depots counted as Army bases. It was meant to last until the first production run was delivered. It is still in force, and the two companies' lobbyists wrote most of its renewals.

nodes.t: United States vs Continental Union, undeclared
nodes.x: A trade dispute over North African partners turned into two weeks of undeclared strikes. US aircraft destroyed Union hydrogen depots and grounded the Écuyer fleet without firing on a single mech. The Union never forgot, and rebuilt its doctrine around never being blind or stranded again. The Union's North African partners drew their own lesson: Strasbourg could not protect them.

nodes.t: United States vs Union over Arctic seabed claims
nodes.x: The first hunter-killer lance action. Pavises jammed a Kestrel flight's landing approach, then shot four of them as they transformed, and a red Castellani Falco finished the rest. Within a year the United States had refitted its front-line Kestrels as Harriers, a heavier design first drawn up against the Pact's rockets. The Union got its first famous ace. Norway, a US ally, watched two allies fight over its own archipelago and began asking which of them would defend it.

nodes.t: The United States unveils its super robots
nodes.x: The United States publicly revealed the Concord class as a deterrent. Every other bloc's hidden program sped up overnight, and every intelligence service started asking who else has one.

nodes.t: Canada asks for observer status in the Union
nodes.x: After the Concord reveal, Canada's parliament learned that its share of the joint North American defence fund had paid for HT-20 plants it was never told about, built by companies that answer to Washington before Ottawa. A motion to seek observer status in the Union passed by eleven votes. Washington called it a procedural matter. Strasbourg sent a delegation the same week.

nodes.t: Canada splits along the Manitoba–Ontario line
nodes.x: Projected. The Halifax Motion's eleven votes become a partition. The western provinces stay with the United States; Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces join the Union, and the United Kingdom, Iceland and Norway follow. Quebec's hydrogen fields come with them, and the Union's fuel cells are never short of hydrogen again. The line between the two Canadas is fought over for the rest of the war.

nodes.t: Mexico joins; Central America and the canal are taken
nodes.x: Projected. Mexico joins the United States, and the canal where Panama once searched every ship is taken with the rest of Central America. It keeps the hemisphere's trade in Washington's hands, and by the war's end the country calls itself the United States of the Americas.

nodes.t: Brazil reaches for Africa and is cut off
nodes.x: Projected. Brazil, flying European frames and trading with Africa, tries to align with the African Union. The Isthmus Seizure cuts the hemisphere in two, US forces push down the Andes and into the Amazon, and the continent becomes a front instead of an ally.

Projected. Refugees from the Canadian Front go north into the Arctic archipelago and Greenland; refugees from the South American Front go south, to Tierra del Fuego and the Antarctic stations. Nobody fights over the ice, which is the point. The communities that survive there learn to live on almost no heat, almost no power and almost no outside help, and stop trusting anyone from the warm places. A few say a giant walked with them across the ice and never said a word. They will carry all of it a very long way.

nodes.t: Places the war is not allowed to enter
nodes.x: Projected. The UN cannot stop the war, so it names the places the war may not enter: Geneva, the hospital ships, the refugee camps on the Falklands, the Antarctic stations, and the roads of the Polar Exodus and the Southern Crossing. Most of the time the fronts go round them, because every side needs somewhere to exchange prisoners, and the white squads are the only people all of them let into the ruins. When a front doesn't go round, the white squads fight whoever it belongs to. At Punta Arenas they hold the harbour for a week against a raiding column sent for the Antarctic stations' fuel, until it turns back. After Vancouver, the UN's casualty count reaches the lunar yards before any bloc's version does.

nodes.t: The Union's council can't agree how to answer Khartoum
nodes.x: When Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia signed the Khartoum Charter, the Union's council needed every member to agree on a response. It met eleven times in four months, could not agree on sanctions, aid or even a statement, and finally issued a communiqué regretting the partners' decision. The Union still has no army of its own: its lances are national contingents, each needing its own parliament's vote to deploy. Strasbourg calls this consensus. Its former partners call it absence. In Marseille, Lyon and Turin, families from the Maghreb who have been Union residents for three generations are starting to be asked which side they are on.

nodes.t: The Secretary-General names the coming war
nodes.x: Months after Mong Hsat, Secretary-General Joaquim Esteves went before the General Assembly with a list: siege trains on the Pact's borders, Concords on parade, a Pact General Staff that no longer meets, a Union council that can't decide anything, Panama opening every container, and warships on the Moon. Every bloc, he said, is preparing for a war it expects someone else to start. He asked for one thing: a standing UN frame force, paid for by every member and answerable to the Assembly. The Assembly voted for it 141 to 9. The Council vetoed its funding three times, once for each bloc. Esteves now asks members for frames one at a time, and more of them are saying yes.

Unmarked frames landed on Yonaguni and Hateruma, two of Japan's outlying Yaeyama Islands. Hayates came ashore through the surf and drove them off in the JSDF's first mech combat. The attackers were never identified. Japan made no accusations and kept selling capacitors to everyone.

nodes.t: Attempted theft of the PT-X Raijin
nodes.x: An infiltration team got inside the Tsukuyomi Lab perimeter before it was stopped. The only one captured was a Grey Lantern contractor who didn't know who had hired them. The Raijin was moved, and Takemikazuchi was hidden deeper.

Beijing asked Mitsurugi for a Mk.III licence and was told the core didn't exist. A week later, Pact customs began holding Japanese capacitor shipments at every port on the Chinese coast. Mitsurugi's board quietly registered subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio and began copying its design archives to both. Licence Diplomacy was built for a world where nobody wanted the factory more than the parts.

Projected. Someone finally decides they would rather have the factory than the parts, and Japan ends the war inside China's sphere. Not all of Mitsurugi goes with it: the subsidiaries in Vladivostok and Ohio take engineers, archives and actuator lines with them. The line that leaves through Russia will go a long way further.

nodes.t: A Russian advance across the Bering Strait
nodes.x: Projected. The Russian half of the Pact Civil War carries its fight across the Bering Strait, and the United States, with little left to stop it, answers with atomic weapons. The limited exchange across the northern front destroys Vancouver. Luna's fleets end the war soon after.

nodes.t: From the Spratly reef to Australia
nodes.x: Projected. The Tieshan-Kai company Tianshu set down on a Spratly reef in 2178 turns out to be the first of many. Chinese landings spread through the Philippines and Indonesia, and American carriers fall back on Australia to hold the line.
Not a conflict. It belongs here because Station Nine, Colony One and the Melas Landing all trace back to what the Ares crew found.
The first station labour dispute. Workers armed Lifter frames with rivet drivers and torches and held a station for a month. Ascension settled, and never fully disarmed them.

nodes.t: Bloc teams fight over a drifting cargo pod
nodes.x: Boarding teams from two blocs reached the same derelict cargo pod near the elevator, and Rigger Security frames fought with harpoons and spike drivers. Three people died, the first combat deaths in orbit. Within months, the blocs had commissioned the first dedicated warships.

nodes.t: A treaty to keep orbit unarmed, vetoed by every bloc
nodes.x: Weeks after the Tether Incident, the UN tabled a treaty to keep orbit unarmed: no warships, no armed frames above the atmosphere, and no reactor-lifted craft in Earth's sky. Each bloc vetoed it, and each commissioned its first warships within months. In the lunar yard someone printed the draft and pinned it up in the crew mess, where it stayed through every bloc's contract. Its third clause becomes the Lunar Mandate's first rule.

nodes.t: A sealed station goes dark for nine hours
nodes.x: Station Nine lost contact for nine hours, the same week Halden activated H-17 in Geneva. Ascension's report blamed a solar flare. There was no flare.

nodes.t: The first permanent settlement on another planet
nodes.x: Ascension's second Mars mission was a settlement, not a landing, and Washington paid most of the bill. Its settlers needed radiation-hardening gene therapy, and US law bars enhanced citizens from federal service, so the Americans among them resigned their commissions and went as Ascension civilians. This year they landed and named their settlement Colony One: the first permanent human home on another planet. Washington insisted on a written charter guaranteeing its oversight, and the settlers are already arguing over the clauses. Their leader is one of the two Ares crew who never gave another interview.

nodes.t: Tianlong's prospecting families keep their own books
nodes.x: Tianlong's orbital subsidiary sent family-crewed tenders out to prospect near-Earth asteroids. Out there, Tianshu's plans arrive late and fit badly, so the crews keep their own ledgers, trade among themselves and settle disputes by reputation. Beijing calls them contractors. They have started calling themselves houses.

nodes.t: Warships in orbit, no doctrine to use them
nodes.x: The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers and Marlinspike frames on their catapults. Nobody has fought with them yet.

nodes.t: Every bloc's warships, built where none of them can claim the slipway
nodes.x: No bloc would let a rival build warships in its own orbit, so the warships are built on the Moon. Ascension's yard sits on a crater rim at the lunar south pole, jointly owned like the elevator ring, and its crews are Ascension's own: many are the children of the Rivet Strike militias. The yard charter swears them to the consortium, not to any bloc, and they build for all of them. Among themselves, they no longer say Ascension. They say lunar.

nodes.t: An unannounced settlement on the site where the Specimen lay
nodes.x: Months after Colony One, an Ascension lander came down in Melas Chasma, in the middle of Valles Marineris, on top of the site where the Ares crew found the Specimen. Its manifest called it a Colony One survey camp; nobody asked Colony One. Its crew came from Station Nine, and they are digging. Halden's scientists, drafting a proposal for a supervised station in the same canyon, don't know one is already there. When Mars is divided, the Red Line between north and south will run straight across it.

nodes.t: The first war fought between ships
nodes.x: Projected. The warships nobody knew how to use learn fast. Fleets fight over the elevators, the solar ring and the lanes to the Moon, and the carriers find that frames win boarding actions but are too slow for open space, so they launch fighter craft beside them. At the Battle of Yernon a single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet, and a Union written off since the European Front is a great power again. The lunar yards build for every side, and watch.

nodes.t: Luna puts its fleets under the UN, and the war stops
nodes.x: Projected. By its last year the war has pushed a biosphere already damaged by two centuries of warming close to collapse, and the atomic exchange over the northern front nearly finishes it. The lunar crews refuse to launch for any bloc. They place the yards, the ring and every ship they crew under the United Nations, the one institution every side had ignored through the war and still let into the ruins, and close the lanes down to Earth until the blocs stop fighting. Its first rule is the third clause of the treaty every bloc vetoed in 2184: nothing lifted by a reactor flies over Earth again. It ends the war and founds the United Nations of Earth and Luna: an institution with its own navy and a mandate to protect humanity from itself, which few asked for and none could refuse.

weapons.label: Weapons
weapons.intro: Mech weapons began as vehicle guns, missiles and construction tools strapped onto walking frames. Two generations later, every bloc has its own branch, and the energy weapons at the end of each branch barely work.
turns: The first mech gun was an IFV cannon with a grip. Within five years every bloc fielded a licensed or stolen copy, which is why Gen 2 mounts worldwide are still sized for it.
Shoulder-mounted tank guns could topple a frame that fired outside its kneeling envelope. Bracing became doctrine, and Pact heavy weapons are still built to fire from a kneel.
Every linear and energy weapon in service traces back to MHI capacitor tech, whether licensed, bought or stolen. Japan's neutrality holds because every bloc depends on it.
The BX-0 fires five shots, then cools for ninety seconds. The plasma blade lasts forty seconds. The Iskra needs a truck. Whoever solves power wins Gen 3.
fams: The workhorse. Every bloc's main gun descends from one US design.
Tank guns that learned to walk. The Pact's speciality.
Infantry and artillery munitions moved onto mechs, from two tubes to forty-rocket salvos.
Construction tools, blades and lances. Where bloc styles differ most.
Railguns and coilguns. A US advantage built on Mitsurugi parts.
Prototypes or defence-only. Nothing here is reliable yet.
Ascension construction equipment, slowly being turned into weapons.

nodes.t: IFV turrets and aircraft gun pods
nodes.x: Chain guns and revolver cannons from infantry fighting vehicles and ground-attack aircraft. Proven, plentiful, and the obvious first thing to hand a mech.

nodes.t: An IFV gun with a pistol grip
nodes.x: The first mech-portable gun to see combat. Brannock-Hale took a stock 30 mm chain gun, added a grip, a shoulder brace and a 120-round box, and shipped it. Crude, but it worked, and every bloc copied it within five years.
The US Army's standard rifle. A bigger round to beat Gen 2 armour, plus a 60 mm underbarrel launcher for bunkers. Rugged enough to use as a club, and pilots do.

VEK licence-built the M30 as the G30, then replaced it. The G35 fires cased-telescoped rounds that burst on command, cued by VEK's sensor suite. Excellent and expensive; supply officers hate the ammunition chain.
Built from M30s captured in a border clash. Tianlong loosened every tolerance and added a 200-round drum. Less accurate than the original, and it keeps firing when caked in mud.

nodes.t: Aircraft gatling built into the arm
nodes.x: OKB-7 skipped the hand-held stage and built an aircraft rotary cannon straight into the forearm. Huge rate of fire, short range, and a frame that can't drop its gun when it runs dry.

nodes.t: Type-07 action, M30 barrel, VEK sight
nodes.x: The League's standard rifle is three rivals' parts on one gun: a licensed Type-07 action, surplus M30 barrels and second-hand VEK optics. Spares are interchangeable with half the black market.

A bridge between chemical and linear guns: a capacitor pulse turns the propellant into plasma for much higher velocity. The Army bought the capacitors straight from Mitsurugi rather than depend on Halcyon. In field trials.
Standard MBT main guns. Enormous recoil, designed to be absorbed by a fifty-tonne hull, not a walking frame.
Shoulder-fired recoilless rifles. No recoil, big back-blast, cheap to make.

nodes.t: A tank gun bolted to the shoulder
nodes.x: Tianlong's first answer to armour: a whole tank gun on the shoulder. Its safe firing envelope required a kneel, and crews who fired standing could be thrown off their feet. Kneeling and bracing became drill, and then doctrine.
America's lighter answer: a scaled-up recoilless rifle. No recoil, a huge back-blast, and the pilot reloads one shell at a time by hand.
The signature Pact weapon. A 200 mm smoothbore carried two-handed, with a folding bipod and a massive muzzle brake. Fired from a kneel at ranges where rifles can't reply.
The M105 grown up: rocket-assisted rounds and a five-round clip. America's main heavy anti-armour weapon, carried in every Brannock fire team.
OKB-7 took the Type-09 concept and added a four-round autoloader, so heavy frames can keep firing while they advance. Too heavy for anything but an OKB-7 chassis.
The League bought retired Type-01s by the hundred and added hydraulic recoil dampers taken from mining rigs. League frames can fire them standing, something Tianlong never managed.

nodes.t: 305 mm, fired from an anchored frame
nodes.x: A siege weapon for OKB-7's new breakthrough frames. The firing mech drives spades into the ground to anchor itself, and a second mech carries the ammunition.
Wire- and laser-guided anti-tank missiles. The shaped-charge warhead technology later spread well beyond missiles.
Area-saturation rocket artillery. Cheap per round and terrifying in volume.

nodes.t: Two infantry missiles on the shoulders
nodes.x: Two standard ATGM tubes strapped to a Gen 1 frame. One shot each, but the first sign that mechs could replace tank destroyers.
Unguided rockets in a cheap rack. Inaccurate alone, but a company firing together hits something.
A twelve-cell shoulder pod that takes anti-armour, anti-air or smoke missiles. Gen 2 mounts everywhere are sized for it.

nodes.t: Fighter missiles on the transforming wings
nodes.x: Halcyon kept its fighter heritage: standard air-to-ground and air-to-air missiles carried on the wing binders and fired in flight mode before landing.
The rocket rack taken to its extreme: forty rockets in a back-mounted battery, emptied in a single salvo, then jettisoned. Every Pact breakthrough opens with one.

nodes.t: Fewer cells, seekers that hunt jammers
nodes.x: A licence-built Hornet with VEK seekers that home on enemy jammers. Fewer cells, a far higher hit rate, and the reason US electronic-warfare pilots fear Continental squadrons.
A copied Hornet casing loaded with cheap Type-03-pattern rockets. It fits US mounts and takes Eurasian ammunition, so League units can buy from whichever bloc is selling.
Hydraulic rams and breakers from demolition and heavy construction.
Heavy cutting tools from forestry and mining machinery.
A demolition ram turned weapon: a hydraulic steel stake that punches through armour at contact range. Slow to cycle, devastating on a hit.
Plate steel with one sharpened edge. It needs no ammunition, which mattered to an army that couldn't count on resupply.
The hydraulics are replaced by explosive blanks in a six-shot cylinder, each one firing the stake. Brannock pilots are close to religious about it.

nodes.t: Shaped-charge tip on a 12 m shaft
nodes.x: A cavalry lance with a missile's shaped-charge warhead in the tip. Paired with the VEK shield it gives Continental mechs their knightly look. Each tip works once.

nodes.t: Layered composite that holds an edge
nodes.x: Layered carbon composite that is lighter and harder than steel and keeps its edge after cutting armour. Cheap to mass-produce, and the Pact's most exported weapon.
Mitsurugi's actuator expertise applied to cutting. The edge vibrates at ultrasonic frequency and saws through armour. It uses a lot of power and wears out quickly.

nodes.t: Licensed HF-1 that stows in the forearm
nodes.x: A shortened, licensed HF-1 that folds into the forearm so it doesn't snag in flight mode. The Kestrel pilot's last resort.

nodes.t: Orbital cutting torch plus MHI capacitors
nodes.x: Castellani combined an Ascension hull-cutting torch with licensed Mitsurugi capacitor cores to make a blade of contained plasma. About forty seconds per charge. The only working unit is assigned to the Union's top ace.
Ship-mounted railgun trials that never quite entered service. Barrels eroded fast and needed a destroyer's power plant.

nodes.t: Built for maglev and factory power
nodes.x: Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every energy weapon since.
The first mech railgun. Power ran through a tether from a backpack capacitor, eight shots per charge. Accurate, and decisive in the battle where it debuted.
An MHI capacitor core inside the stock removed the tether. Thirty shots per battery pack, and the hypervelocity rounds go through Gen 2 armour easily. America's main technological edge.
Mitsurugi's own design. Lower velocity than the LR-3 but much more reliable, and the capacitor core inside it is the most licensed component in the world.
Built from LR-1 plans obtained through espionage. It works, but barrel erosion forces a change every forty shots. Issued only to elite Pact units.
A licensed Type-L stretched into a long-range coilgun for the Pavise. VEK fuel cells recharge it slowly, so it is used as a single-shot precision weapon.
Ground- and ship-based lasers that shoot down missiles. Building-sized, grid-powered, and far too weak to hurt armour.
A shoulder laser that destroys incoming missiles, drawing from the Kestrel's linear-rifle packs. The first energy weapon in squadron service, and defensive only.

Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype particle beam rifle. Five shots that go through any armour, then ninety seconds to cool while it erodes its own barrel liner. It has never finished a trial without a fault, and every bloc wants it.
OKB-7's brute-force answer: a particle cannon fed by cable from a generator truck. Immobile while firing, but nothing on the battlefield hits harder.
Pneumatic and explosive rivet drivers used to assemble station hulls.
High-power plasma torches for cutting thick plate.
The magnetic track that throws cargo pods off the orbital elevators. The largest electromagnetic accelerator ever built.

nodes.t: Worker-frame tool, first used in anger
nodes.x: The standard hull-riveting tool on Ascension worker frames. It became a weapon during the first station labour dispute, when workers turned it on security frames.
The worker frame's hull cutter. Ascension sold the design to Castellani, which turned it into a sword.
A salvage tug's harpoon and winch. Militarised versions grapple and board, which is how most fights in orbit actually end.
A militarised RD-9 firing tungsten spikes, with recoil balanced against the frame so it doesn't send the shooter tumbling in zero gravity. Officially still a construction tool.

nodes.t: Main gun of the first warships
nodes.x: A shortened section of elevator launch track fitted as the main gun of the first dedicated warships, built with Halcyon linear-rifle know-how under contract.

power.label: Power
power.intro: Every mech is short on power, and each bloc made a different trade. Brannock and Tianlong accepted noise and heat for endurance. Halcyon accepted forty minutes for silence. VEK accepted a hydrogen supply chain. Mitsurugi supplies the capacitors everyone else depends on.
turns: Brannock's turbine plumes showed on thermal sights kilometres away. Halcyon chose quiet, cool batteries and accepted forty minutes of endurance.
The swap pit became a battlefield
Ninety-second battery swaps made US ground crews a front-line arm, and made swap points a target.
VEK's quiet fuel cells needed depots, which became targets. The BZ-6 reformer fixed it by making hydrogen from ordinary diesel.
Fission (OKB-7), fusion (Mitsurugi) and beamed power (Ascension and Halcyon). Each one is a political crisis waiting to happen.
fams: Turbines and diesels. Loud, hot and dependable.
Silent and cool-running, but endurance is measured in minutes.
Quiet hydrogen power. The problem is the hydrogen.
Pulse power for linear and energy weapons. Almost all of it is Mitsurugi's.
Prototypes only. Unlimited endurance, unacceptable consequences.
Orbital power that could reach the ground.

nodes.x: Multi-fuel gas turbines from main battle tanks. Compact and powerful, but they drink fuel and leave a hot exhaust plume.
Diesel engines from heavy trucks and locomotives. Heavy, low-tech, and repairable anywhere.

nodes.t: A tank turbine in a mech torso
nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's first frames ran on a modified tank turbine. Plenty of power and hours of fuel, but an exhaust plume thermal sights could see for kilometres.
A truck diesel turning a generator that feeds the limb motors. Heavy and loud, but any village mechanic can fix it. This is why Tianlong frames have such big torsos.

nodes.t: Battery for sprints, turbine to cruise
nodes.x: A smaller turbine paired with a buffer battery. The mech sprints on battery, cruises on the turbine, and can shut the turbine down to cut its heat signature in an ambush. Brannock engineers won't admit the battery work came from Halcyon.
A tougher diesel that runs on almost any liquid fuel, including captured stocks and refinery waste. It's the main reason Pact armies need so little logistics.
OKB-7 heavy frames carry two Type-06-derived engines. One can fail and the frame still walks home. It powers the Molot autoloader and Grad-M ignition circuits.
Surplus GT-900 turbines rebuilt to burn the League's own refinery output, with Type-06 fuel pumps grafted on. Hot and dirty, but the League makes all of its own fuel.

nodes.t: Mobile power for weapons too big for a mech
nodes.x: A wheeled generator built around four D-40 engines. It feeds the Iskra particle cannon by cable and recharges forward units. It's the first thing enemy pilots target.

nodes.t: Turbine charging an MHI capacitor bank
nodes.x: The frame-sized version of the plant Joint Heavy Systems first built at super-heavy scale for the Concord, and the power behind the AR-40E rifle. The turbine charges a licensed Mitsurugi capacitor bank, giving the Army pulse power without Halcyon's battery packs. Shrinking it to fit a 17 m frame is the hard part.
Lithium-chemistry cells developed for electric vehicles and grid storage.

nodes.t: Fixed pack, forty minutes per charge
nodes.x: Halcyon's first frames used a fixed battery in the spine driving electric fans: quiet and cool-running, with no exhaust plume for thermal sights to find, but hours to recharge. Short endurance became part of US doctrine.
A pack a ground crew can swap in ninety seconds with a frame-mounted crane. It made the swap pit a combat position and turned ground crews into a combat arm.
Mitsurugi's design for Self-Defence Force frames: modest batteries with a large capacitor stage for bursts. Less endurance than Halcyon's packs, much better for energy weapons.

nodes.t: MHI capacitor buffer for the LR-3
nodes.x: Higher-density cells plus a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer that feeds the LR-3 rifle and PL-2 laser. The current Kestrel standard, and America's most export-restricted part.
Hydrogen fuel cells from air-independent submarines and city buses.
VEK's first frames used a fuel cell adapted from submarines. Near-silent and cold-running, but it needs hydrogen depots, and those became US strike targets.
Cells come in stackable modules, so a frame carrying heavy packs can carry extra power too. This is what makes the modular task group possible. Expensive, and very sensitive to contamination.

nodes.t: Makes its own hydrogen from diesel
