nodes.x: Adds a reformer that strips hydrogen from ordinary diesel. Less efficient and slightly louder, but frames can now refuel from any truck, ending the depot problem.
Castellani's hand-built stacks run at 140% of rated output. Spectacular performance, about two hundred hours before replacement, and only fitted to named aces' mechs.
In orbit, hydrogen comes from water, which stations already recycle. Ascension's worker frames ran on fuel cells from the start.

nodes.t: Fuel cell with fold-out solar wings
nodes.x: Folding solar panels recharge the frame's electrolysers between shifts, so a worker frame can stay out for days. The militarised versions keep that endurance.
Before mechs, Mitsurugi built high-density capacitor banks for maglev lines and heavy industry. That product line turned out to be the key to every energy weapon since.
The first mech-portable capacitor, sold to Halcyon for the LR-1 rifle. Large enough to need its own backpack.

nodes.t: The most licensed part in the world
nodes.x: Small enough to fit in a rifle stock. It's inside the LR-3, Type-L and PL-2, and is licensed or copied by every bloc. Japan's neutrality depends on it.
Licence-built Mk.II cores for the Spiegel coilgun and Castellani's projects. Mitsurugi deliberately sells VEK one generation behind.
Reverse-engineered from a captured Mk.I. It works, at twice the weight and half the charge life. Only elite Type-12 rail units get them.
Tsukuyomi Lab's prototype for the BX-0 beam rifle. It stores enough for five beam shots, and its discharge heat is why the rifle needs ninety seconds to cool.
US pressurised-water reactors from submarines and carriers. Reliable at sea, enormous by mech standards.

nodes.t: A shielded mini-reactor in a heavy frame
nodes.x: OKB-7's secret test frame carries a shielded micro-reactor. Unlimited endurance on paper. In practice the pilot's radiation dose is measured, and every bloc fears what happens when one is shot down over a city.
Decades of laboratory fusion work. Never net-positive outside a building-sized facility.

nodes.t: Too big for any normal frame; Japan's best-kept secret
nodes.x: Tsukuyomi Lab's compact fusion rig, using Mk.II capacitor tech for the ignition pulse. Far too big for a normal frame: the only mech that carries one is Takemikazuchi, built at 45 m to fit it. If it ever shrinks to fit an 18 m frame, the balance of power changes overnight.
Photovoltaic arrays powering satellites and early stations.
Huge collectors around the elevator anchors that power the cargo launch tracks and stations. The largest power source in orbit, jointly owned by every bloc.
Ascension's experiment in beaming surplus ring power to ground receivers. Officially for disaster relief. Every military noticed it could recharge a mech.

nodes.t: Kestrels recharged by beam, never landing
nodes.x: Halcyon's classified program to recharge QX-3 packs from an Ascension relay mid-flight. Halcyon frames fly on electric fans, so beamed power keeps both the fans and the weapons running. If it works, America's forty-minute limit disappears, and there's a weapon-grade power beam over every battlefield.

doctrine.label: Doctrine
doctrine.intro: Each bloc's doctrine follows from its hardware and its constraints. The United States fights on a forty-minute battery clock, the Union blinds the enemy to make up for small numbers, and the Pact spends frames to save time. The rest improvise.
turns: Every bloc first used mechs to kill tanks, not other mechs. Mech-on-mech doctrine came later than anyone expected.
US drop-and-strike runs on battery endurance. The Union and Pact both built counter-doctrines around surviving the first forty minutes.
The Union's EW-led doctrine makes up for its small numbers. It's the main reason Continental lances punch above their weight.
Beijing's Tianshu network runs the walls and the Air Umbrella; Moscow runs the breakthrough groups and the augmented pilots. Pact doctrine is becoming two doctrines.
Nobody knows how to fight in orbit
Warships exist; space doctrine doesn't. The first real battle in orbit will rewrite every manual.
fams: Expeditionary forces. Speed, air power and a long Army–Air Force rivalry.
Small numbers, high quality. Blind the enemy, then fight.
Mass, firepower and acceptable losses. Beijing builds walls; Moscow builds breakthroughs.
Defensive by law, influential by industry, and running out of room.
Making do with everyone else's equipment.
Fighting where nobody has doctrine yet.
Borrowed frames from every bloc, and strict rules for when they may fire.

nodes.t: Armour holds, air power strikes deep
nodes.x: Pre-mech US doctrine: armour holds the front while air power strikes deep behind it.
Infantry delivered by helicopter and tiltrotor behind or around the enemy front.
The Army's first mech doctrine. Pairs of Brannock frames with M30s and ATGM tubes ambushed tanks from terrain tanks couldn't cross, then fell back to friendly armour.
Early Halcyon ground frames were carried under tiltrotors and dropped behind enemy lines. Effective, but the tiltrotors were easy kills, which pushed Halcyon toward transformation.

nodes.t: Four-mech teams replace tanks in rough terrain
nodes.x: Four Brannock frames per team: two rifles, one Hornet pod, one M140 bazooka. Fire teams now replace tanks in mountains, forests and cities.

nodes.t: Fly in, land, fight, leave inside forty minutes
nodes.x: Kestrels fly in, strike with wing stores, land and fight with LR-3s, then transform and leave before their batteries run out. The forty-minute clock drives every plan; enemies call it “the forty-minute war”.

nodes.t: Army holds the ground, Air Force strikes
nodes.x: After years of rivalry, a joint mandate: Brannock fire teams seize and hold a swap point, and Kestrels strike from it. The services still argue over who commands.

nodes.t: Forward battery points as combat positions
nodes.x: Battery-swap pits within reach of the front. Ground crews are trained and armed as combat troops, and enemies now target pits before mechs.

nodes.t: Kestrels that never need to land
nodes.x: A draft doctrine written for the SKYLINE beamed-power program: Kestrels that stay airborne for hours. It doesn't work without SKYLINE, and nobody knows whether SKYLINE works.

nodes.t: Two ordinary soldiers, not one altered one
nodes.x: America's answer to the Volk and to the rumours about Koschei. Every US pilot serves unaltered, by regulation, and recruits are screened for implants. Halcyon and Brannock-Hale advertise their frames as built for ordinary people, and the Concord's two-pilot crew is presented as proof. In Washington, biological purity is starting to sound like patriotism.
European armoured cavalry: fast reconnaissance units that find and fix the enemy for the main force.
Cold War electronic warfare: jamming, deception and signals intelligence.

nodes.t: Licensed frames scouting ahead of tanks
nodes.x: The first Union mechs, licensed Brannock frames, screened ahead of tank columns, using their height and sensors to see farther than vehicles could.
The standard hardpoint means a lance of three VEK frames can be re-equipped for assault, defence or recon overnight. It makes up for the Union's small numbers.
Every engagement opens with electronic attack: jam the sensors, spoof the data links, then attack while the enemy is blind. EW frames lead formations instead of following them.

nodes.t: EW frame, coilgun sniper, lance knight
nodes.x: Built to defeat drop-and-strike. An EW frame jams the Kestrels' landing approach, a Spiegel sniper shoots them as they transform, and a lance-armed frame finishes them on the ground.
The Union gives its best prototypes to famous aces and publicises their kills. Part morale, part propaganda, and part a way to sell member states on more spending.

nodes.t: Every program answers to a panel that can stop it
nodes.x: When the Union's parliament learned, from footage Geneva sent every member on the same morning, what Halden had sent into the Great Sand Sea in its name, it put every defence research program under an ethics panel with the power to halt it. Halden's Geneva laboratories are the panel's first case, and the hearings are still running. The Union is slower for it, and intends to stay that way.
Offensives in successive echelons, each wave exploiting the gap the last one opened.
Artillery as the arm that decides battles, used in enormous concentrations.

nodes.t: Six weeks of training, many frames
nodes.x: The Pact accepted early on that Tianlong frames were outclassed, and fields so many that the enemy runs out of ammunition first. Pilots train for six weeks.
Type-01 cannons could only fire braced, so mechs formed kneeling firing lines like artillery batteries. A technical workaround became the Pact's defining image.
Three waves: the first empties Grad-M batteries, the second kneels and fires Type-09s, the third closes with carbon blades. Each wave is timed to arrive as the one before runs dry.

nodes.t: Dug-in kneeling lines on the borders
nodes.x: Type-09 lines in prepared positions along the borders, mechs dug in to the shoulders. Very hard to dislodge, and the reason no bloc has invaded the Pact. Since 2180, Tianshu has decided which sector the reserves go to.
OKB-7 heavy frames with Molot cannons lead and punch a hole for the waves behind. The first change in Pact doctrine that values quality over numbers.

nodes.t: Engineered elites for the best frames
nodes.x: Conscript losses made elite pilots precious. The answer is Department Zero, a secret institute that augments pilots with implants and conditioning. Officially it doesn't exist. It is run from Moscow. Beijing's planners accept cybernetic links but refuse anything that rewrites the pilot, and say so at every staff meeting.

Built to defeat drop-and-strike: Type-03 racks loaded with anti-air rockets fire massed volleys over fortress belts to deny landing zones. Cheap, crude and effective. Its batteries are cued by Tianshu, Beijing's planning network and the most automated command system any bloc has fielded.

nodes.t: Mongolian crews who scout ahead of the frame trains
nodes.x: Tianshu can route a frame train across Mongolia, but it can't see the pasture, the washed-out crossings or the herders who know both. Since the Fortress Belt went in, Mongolian and Kazakh crews have scouted the rail lines in stripped-down Tieniu, living in their frames for weeks between depots. They are austere, communal and the least predictable part of Tianshu's plans: they treat a frame like a horse, and don't leave a lame one behind. Beijing calls them the Steppe detachments.
Draft doctrine for breaking fortified cities with siege mortars and cable-fed particle cannons. It assumes a long war, which is what worries the other blocs most.

nodes.t: The network proposes, the officer approves
nodes.x: Tianshu began as Tianlong's rail scheduler for the frame trains, grew into the planner behind the Fortress Belt, and learned to cue the Air Umbrella. Under Order 21 it drafts every operational plan from sensors, depot stocks and rail timetables, and officers approve or amend it. Officers who amend too often are retrained. Tianshu also grades them for reliability, and nobody outside Beijing knows what it measures. Moscow's staff officers call it command by forecast.
A long-standing legal limit: Japanese forces exist only to defend Japan.
Decades of national strategy built on high-value manufacturing exports.
Japan's first mechs were rescue and recovery frames for earthquakes and tsunamis. The public trusted mechs before the military armed them.

nodes.t: Coasts and islands, with the navy
nodes.x: Self-Defence Force frames defend coastlines and outlying islands, deployed from amphibious ships with naval fire support. Type-L carbines and HC-2 hybrid cells.

nodes.t: Sell to everyone, depend on no one
nodes.x: Japan's real defence doctrine: license critical parts to every bloc so no one can afford to attack the supplier. It works as long as no bloc decides it would rather seize the factory.
Selected JSDF units take Mitsurugi prototypes into live exercises and the occasional real incident. The fastest test cycle in the world, and why so many prototypes end up in combat.
Irregular warfare built around armed pickup trucks and local militia.
A shared refusal to join any of the major blocs.

nodes.t: Surplus Gen 1 frames as militia fire support
nodes.x: The League's first mechs were surplus Gen 1 frames supporting militia, the mech equivalent of a gun on a pickup. They taught a generation of pilots to improvise.
Small groups hide in dunes and sandstorms, strike convoys and depots, then scatter. The League rarely wins a pitched battle, so it avoids them.
League states deny bases to every bloc and keep enough mechs to make an incursion costly. The blocs fight proxy wars here instead.
League battalions mix frames from every bloc, organised around which parts interchange. Borrowed from the Continental modular idea, but driven by supply instead of choice.

The Khartoum Charter's doctrine, written after the Jinn sightings. Frames are positioned to shield populations rather than to hold ground, and a battalion's first duty in any fight is evacuation. The Gulf associates call it soft. The Charter states point out that people still live in the Great Sand Sea.
Security on early stations was policing: no heavy weapons, no military chain of command.
Centuries of ship-to-ship combat doctrine, none of it written for orbit.
Private firms hired to guard assets in unstable regions.

nodes.t: Armed worker frames after the labour dispute
nodes.x: After the first station labour dispute, Ascension crews formed armed militias with rivet drivers and torches. The consortium never fully disarmed them.
Most fights in orbit end with a harpoon and a cut hull, because nobody wants to destroy the station they're fighting over. Worker frames do it better than military ones.

nodes.t: Small elite teams, the best of every bloc
nodes.x: Grey Lantern Security fields small teams using the best frame from each bloc. It copied the US fire-team structure, then threw out the rules of engagement.

The white squads' first rules of engagement, written for the convoy escorts. A white frame fires only to protect a convoy, a camp or itself, never pursues, and never holds ground for anyone. Squads train to fight as mixed units whose frames share no parts, and their mechanics learn every bloc's wiring.

Rewritten after Mong Hsat. When the Security Council names a threat to civilians, a white squad may go after it instead of waiting for it, and may finish it. Esteves calls it the narrowest possible exception. The squads who flew at Mong Hsat call it the Sawbwa rule.
The first dedicated warships carry mass drivers and mech catapults, but nobody has fought ship-to-ship in orbit. Every bloc is borrowing old naval thinking and hoping.

vehicles.label: Vehicles
vehicles.intro: Tanks, jets and helicopters didn't disappear when mechs arrived. They're cheaper, lower and harder to see than a 17 m frame, so every line adapted instead: roof armour and high-angle guns for tanks, escort and hunting roles for fighters, mast sights and fire-and-forget missiles for gunships. Later models borrow mech technology as it matures, from capacitor cores to point-defence lasers. The one role that did end is marked END.
turns: Garrisons ambushed a TL-80 column from a ravine tanks couldn't climb. Designers answered with roof armour, high-angle guns and hull-down tactics. A tank is 2.4 m tall and costs a quarter as much as a Teamster.
A mech can see over every ridge, but everyone can see a mech. Low vehicles became the ambushers: hull-down tanks, recon cars in hedgerows, and gunships just below the crest line.

A Kestrel is a ground frame that can fly, and a poor dogfighter. Fighters escort the drops, other fighters hunt them, and jets with hours of fuel fly the support missions a forty-minute battery can't.
Capacitor cores, electrothermal guns and point-defence lasers were built for frames, and they're now going into tanks, fighters and gunships. The BH-110 Regulator and the Kite IV are the result.
fams: Escorts, hunters, and jets that can stay longer than forty minutes.
Under the crest line, where a mech can't follow.

nodes.x: Brannock-Hale's main battle tank: gas turbine, 125 mm gun, composite armour, and the fire-control system that later went into the Garrison. On open ground it was the best tank in the world.

nodes.t: Roof armour and a sensor mast after Iron Gate
nodes.x: Iron Gate showed what happens when the enemy fires from above. The A3 added roof armour against plunging fire, a sensor mast to see over ridges, and a gun that elevates far enough to hit a mech's torso. Crews learned to stay hull-down and let the frames give themselves away first.

nodes.t: The first tank designed to fight mechs
nodes.x: A low hull, heavy roof armour, a high-angle 125 mm gun, and a roof-mounted Hornet pod for shots at hip actuators. On open plains a Marshal II platoon costs about as much as one Teamster and spots a frame long before the frame finds it. Brannock fire teams own rough ground; Marshals own flat ground.

nodes.t: Point-defence laser borrowed from the Harrier
nodes.x: Hornet pods and Grad-M salvos made the roof the weak spot again. The A2 mounts a PL-2-derived laser on the turret to shoot down incoming missiles, fed from a capacitor buffer the turbine charges.

nodes.t: An electrothermal gun on a tank
nodes.x: A Marshal successor built around the HT-20 plant and an enlarged AR-40E electrothermal gun. It hits about as hard as a linear rifle, from a hull 2.4 m tall. The Army's mech lobby calls it a waste of capacitors. The tank lobby points out that it costs a quarter as much as a Pathfinder.

nodes.t: “Iron Armour”: cheap, low, exported by the thousand
nodes.x: Tianlong's mass-production tank: small, simple, and sold across Africa and Arabia. An insurgent column of them was the first armour ever destroyed by mechs, at Iron Gate. Thousands are still in service.

nodes.t: Taught to fight beside the Tieniu
nodes.x: After Iron Gate the Pact kept building tanks and taught them to work with mechs. Tiejia platoons guard the Tieniu's legs and flanks while the frames kneel to fire, and a raised gun mount lets them hit a frame's torso at close range. Cheap, plentiful and easy to crew.

nodes.t: Autoloader, reactive roof armour, export favourite
nodes.x: Built in the same factories as the Tieshan, on the same multi-fuel diesel. Reactive armour on the roof stops the plunging fire that kills older tanks, and the autoloader fires fast enough to hit a mech before it ducks back behind a ridge. The most exported tank in the world.

nodes.t: Fights in the gaps between kneeling Tieshans
nodes.x: Order 11 waves leave gaps between kneeling frames, and the TL-19 fills them. It's low and fast, with top-attack missiles in the turret and a Type-07 action as its coaxial gun. Every Tieshan company now has a Tiejia platoon assigned to protect its legs.

nodes.t: Turretless Tiejia hull, raid supply carrier
nodes.x: The League bought surplus TL-92s, cut off the turrets, and turned them into armoured carriers for fuel, ammunition and frame parts. The frames do the fighting, and the Kafila keeps them running between strikes. One convoy of them keeps the Jinn alive.

nodes.t: TL-99 hull with a refurbished shoulder cannon
nodes.x: The League's own tank: a surplus TL-99 hull carrying a Type-01Q cannon on mining-rig recoil dampers. It fires on the move, which no Tianlong vehicle ever managed with that gun, and it hides in dunes a Sirocco couldn't crouch behind.

nodes.t: Light enough for mountain bridges and landing ships
nodes.x: Japan's defensive tank, built light for mountain roads and amphibious ships. Mitsurugi's suspension work on it fed into the balance-control research behind every later MHI frame.

nodes.t: Wheeled, fast, shipped with the Hayates
nodes.x: Japan replaced the Type-78 with an eight-wheeled combat vehicle that rides the same landing ships as the Hayates. On island roads it outruns a frame, and its coil gun, derived from the Type-L, makes any intruder's mech think twice. The Hayates hold the beach; the Type-11s hold the roads behind it.
A light tank built to go under a tiltrotor with airborne infantry: thin armour and a 105 mm gun.

The Sparrowhawk took over the air-drop job, so the Army found the Ranger a new one. A low, fast tank with ATGMs in the turret can hide where a 17 m frame can't, and wait for a Tieniu to walk past. Ranger crews call it fighting from the ankles.

Two metres tall, quiet on hybrid drive, with a mast sight and top-attack missiles aimed at hip actuators. Hounds work in pairs ahead of a fire team, finding enemy frames and forcing them to stop and deal with something they can barely see.

nodes.t: The fire team's hidden fifth member
nodes.x: Data-linked to Teamster fire teams, so a Hound can fire Hornet cells at targets a Teamster has marked, and the other way round. Fire teams that train with a Hound pair lose fewer frames than teams that don't, which has quietly settled the argument about whether tanks still matter.

nodes.t: Wheeled recon with a telescoping sensor mast
nodes.x: The Union's reconnaissance car: fast, quiet, with a mast that raised its sensors eight metres.

A mech sees farther from 17 m up, but it can be seen from everywhere. The Genette-B went passive: no radar, a low mast and thermal sights, so it could sit in a hedgerow and watch what the Écuyer screen could only guess at.

Directive 5 opens every fight with electronic attack, and the Genette-E delivers it from closer than any aircraft dares. It creeps to within a few kilometres of the enemy line, switches on, and moves before anyone can find it.

nodes.t: A decoy that looks like a lance
nodes.x: Built for the hunter-killer lance: a car that broadcasts the radar and radio signature of a Pavise. Enemy Kestrels see three lances where there's one, and the Genette-L doesn't mind being shot at, as long as it keeps moving.
America's infantry carrier: six dismounts in the back and a 30 mm chain gun on top. That chain gun, given a pistol grip, became the M30, the first mech weapon.

nodes.t: Up-armoured to keep up with mechs
nodes.x: Infantry still clear buildings and guard frames at rest. The A4 added armour and a frame-height periscope so its crew could follow a Garrison pair through ground the old Drover avoided.
One Drover II rides with each four-mech fire team, carrying dismounts, M140 reloads and spare stake-driver cylinders. It's the reason a Brannock team can fight for a day without falling back.

nodes.t: Armoured swap-pit carrier with a battery crane
nodes.x: A Drover II hull with the M1100's flatbed: four QX-3 packs under armour, a fold-out crane, and a 30 mm turret for when the pit is attacked. Kestrels land beside it, swap in ninety seconds and leave. Pit crews call it the most shot-at vehicle in the Army.

nodes.t: A swap pit with no crew
nodes.x: Enemies target swap pits before they target mechs, so the Army is testing a Pitwagon with no crew. It drives to a grid reference, opens up, and swaps packs on its own. It works in trials. In its one live test, it was the first thing destroyed.
The backbone of Pact massed artillery. Before mechs, batteries of these decided battles.
Order 5's kneeling lines took over direct fire, but indirect fire still needed tubes. The TL-90 added an autoloader and shoot-and-move drills, because mech raids could now reach the gun lines.

nodes.t: Rocket artillery behind the fortress belt
nodes.x: Tracked rocket launchers alongside the tube guns: cheaper, quicker to move, and enough to break up an assault on a fortress belt before it reaches the kneeling lines.

nodes.t: “Watchtower”: radar and fire control for the Air Umbrella
nodes.x: A Leiting chassis with a folding radar and the fire-control link that makes Order 19 work. It cues hundreds of Tiebi rocket racks onto a Kestrel flight's landing approach at once. It's the only Pact vehicle with a higher protection priority than the mechs. Its fire-control link was the first time Tianshu aimed weapons rather than trains.

nodes.t: Tank transporter trucks and rail flats
nodes.x: Tanks wear out their tracks on long drives, so armies moved them by truck and rail. Mechs turned out to wear out their knees even faster.

nodes.t: Low-loader for a Garrison lying on its back
nodes.x: A Garrison walks at 30 km/h and needs new knee bearings every few hundred kilometres, so the US Army moves frames by road, lying flat on these. Every US frame since has had lift points for it.

nodes.t: Tracked, armoured carrier for a kneeling Tieshan
nodes.x: The M1100 idea on armoured TL-92 running gear. A Tieshan kneels on the back and rides to the line, saving its legs for the fight. Pact frame companies arrive by carrier, step off the back, and are firing within a minute.

nodes.t: Follows Koschei on tracks, feeding it by cable
nodes.x: Frame-carrier running gear scaled up until it can carry a micro-reactor and an MTU-7 generator stack. It follows Koschei on its own tracks. The cable between them is the one part Department Zero can't armour.
The fighter whose wing binders, avionics and flight-control software every Halcyon frame inherited. It ruled the air in the decade before mechs.

nodes.t: Escort for the first variable frames
nodes.x: Built on the same line as the Merlin. The Merlin could fly but couldn't dogfight, so Gyrfalcon IIs escorted every Merlin flight and dealt with interceptors while the frames transformed and landed. Escorting frames became the American fighter's main job.

Designed around a Kestrel's two worst moments: landing and take-off. Lanners hold the air over a landing zone for forty minutes, then cover the climb-out. In the Forty-Minute War they kept Kestrel losses low, until the Pact's advisers switched to hitting the swap pits.

nodes.t: Laser defence on a capacitor bank
nodes.x: After the Sapsan, escort fighters had to survive rocket salvos too. The Saker carries a PL-2-derived laser and a Mitsurugi capacitor buffer charged by its engines, the first fighter to run on mech power technology. Saker pilots train alongside the Harriers they escort.
A slow, armoured jet built around a rotary cannon for killing tanks, with hours of loiter time.

A mech is the tallest thing on the battlefield and can't hide in a fold of ground. Shrikes were rearmed with heavier cannon rounds and top-attack bombs aimed at hip and knee actuators, and flew low enough to stay under early mechs' sensors.

nodes.t: Hours of support a Kestrel can't give
nodes.x: Kestrels raid; Shrikes stay. With hours of fuel against a Kestrel's forty minutes, the Shrike II flies the long support missions, firing glide munitions from beyond Hornet range. The Army asks for Shrikes by name, which the Air Force pretends not to notice.
Before it built mechs, Kirov-Mikoyan OKB-7 was a fighter bureau. The Strizh was built to catch US bombers, and the bureau's heavy, aggressive engineering carried straight into the Medved.
Re-radared to find mechs moving through broken ground. At the Talysh Mountains it found the Merlins too late: they had already transformed and gone.

Designed after the Forty-Minute War around one number: the two seconds a Kestrel spends half-folded, too slow to fly and too high to fight. Sapsans circle over landing zones and dive into that window with short-range missiles. With the Air Umbrella, they're why the Harrier carries a point-defence laser.

nodes.t: Rocket salvos too big for one laser
nodes.x: OKB-7's answer to the Harrier: rocket salvos too large for one PL-2 to stop, and a dive that clears the landing zone before the Harriers' wingmen can reply.
A good, expensive European fighter, bought in small numbers by every Union member.

nodes.t: Lost the Maghreb air battle, changed jobs
nodes.x: In the Maghreb Depot Strikes, US pilots out-flew the Hirondelles and destroyed the Union's hydrogen depots in two weeks. The Union stopped trying to beat the Americans fighter for fighter, and rebuilt the Hirondelle around jamming instead of dogfighting.

A two-seat electronic-attack fighter, with jammers in place of half its missiles and a back-seater who blinds enemy radar before the Haubert lances move. It scores fewer kills than the old Hirondelle and has far more influence on the fight.

The air half of Directive 8. Martinets wait over a Kestrel flight's predicted landing zone, cued by Pavise jammers on the ground, and attack the Kestrels on approach. The Spiegels take the ones that make it down.
OKB-7's intercontinental cruise-missile carrier.

nodes.t: Standoff missiles for swap pits and carriers
nodes.x: The Forty-Minute War showed the Pact where the United States is weakest: the swap pits and the carriers that feed its Kestrels. The Lebed-M fires long-range missiles at both from far outside US fighter cover.
A converted airliner with a rotating radar dome and jamming pods: the eyes of Union air defence.

nodes.t: Rebuilt as a flying jammer after Maghreb
nodes.x: After the Maghreb strikes the Argus fleet was rebuilt for electronic attack, with fewer radars and far more jammers. It flew the first Directive 5 engagements, blinding enemy sensors before the Écuyers moved.
Data links to every Haubert lance and enough jamming power to blind a division. It was also the biggest, slowest target over any battlefield, and the Air Umbrella proved it.

Once Pavises could jam from the ground, the Argus moved to high altitude far behind the line. It no longer jams the enemy. It ties every lance, Pavise and Martinet into one picture, which is a harder job to replace.
Halcyon's four-engine transport, built to carry tanks to wars across an ocean.
A strengthened floor and a longer ramp let it carry one Garrison or Sparrowhawk across an ocean. America's whole expeditionary model depended on them.

nodes.t: Frame airlifter: three Kestrels or two Teamsters
nodes.x: The first airlifter designed around mechs, with a nose and tail that both open so frames can walk straight through. Rough-strip landing gear lets it land close enough to the front to matter. It exists because the Heron Heavy proved that frames slung under rotors get shot down.

nodes.t: A swap pit that flies in
nodes.x: A Condor that lands on a road, lowers both ramps and becomes a swap pit, with forty QX-3 packs, two cranes and an Osprey aboard. It's gone again within the hour. Sapsan pilots hunt Condor Pits as hard as they hunt Kestrels.

nodes.t: Re-beams orbital power to Kestrels under the clouds
nodes.x: A Condor airframe with a rectenna on top and a transmitter underneath. It catches power from Ascension's microwave relay above the weather and passes it down to SKYLINE Harriers. If it works, the forty-minute clock lasts as long as the relay stays up.
Halcyon's attack helicopter. It hid behind ridges, popped up to fire missiles, and dropped back down.

nodes.t: A mast sight above the ridge, the rest below it
nodes.x: A mech's sensor head sees over the ridges Kites used to hide behind. The HH-52's answer was a mast-mounted sight, so only a ball the size of a football shows above the crest while the airframe stays hidden. After that, Kites found Tieniu more often than Tieniu found Kites.

nodes.t: Fire-and-forget missiles aimed at the knees
nodes.x: Kite IIIs escort Brannock fire teams and hunt enemy frames from behind, aiming at knee and hip actuators to leave a frame stranded rather than destroyed. Hornet anti-air pods keep them low and careful, but they're still the fastest anti-mech weapon a commander can call in.

nodes.t: Quiet hybrid drive and a point-defence laser
nodes.x: The first gunship built with mech technology: an HT-12-style hybrid drive that lets it hover on batteries with the turbines throttled back, and a small PL-2-derived laser to shoot down anti-air rockets. It's the only rotorcraft with a chance under the Air Umbrella.
Halcyon's tiltrotor, carrying airborne infantry with a Ranger light tank slung underneath.

A heavy-lift Heron built to sling a stripped-down Sparrowhawk. In the Tiltrotor Drops at the end of Iron Gate the frames did well and the Herons did not: nine were shot down in a month. Halcyon's answer was a mech that could fly itself in. The airframe stayed in service; the role didn't.
nodes.z: 2166 · frame drops end; the Merlin flies itself in

nodes.t: Flies battery packs to the swap pits
nodes.x: Herons stopped carrying frames and started carrying what frames need. A Pit Runner slings four QX packs or a load of LR-3 magazines to a forward swap pit, and leaves before anyone starts shooting at the pit.
Big enough to lift a light tank. A 72-tonne Tieniu was another matter.
It can't lift a frame, so it lifts everything else: replacement legs, Type-01 shells and rocket racks, flown straight to kneeling lines the trucks can't reach.
Bigger rotors and an underslung cradle for Grad-M batteries, so a wave's first salvo can be reloaded within the hour. Pact crews call it the second salvo.
A small, quiet scout helicopter that spotted for Union armoured cavalry.

The Colibri flies below the treeline behind the Écuyers and lifts a mast sight over the trees to look where they're looking. It's smaller and quieter than any frame, and it sees what a mech's own height gives away.
A Colibri with a jamming pod, flying low over a Union lance to extend its electronic attack. It's cheap enough to lose, which is the point.
OKB-7's heavy assault helicopter: armoured, rocket-armed, and able to carry a squad in the back.

OKB-7's answer to the Kite: a heavily armoured gunship that flies just behind Order 11 waves, firing rockets into whatever the kneeling lines flush out. It trusts its armour more than its sights, which suits Pact crews.
Built to fly under the Pact's own rocket umbrella, with identification gear the Wanglou trusts. It hunts Kestrels in the few seconds after they land, when they're down but not yet ready to fight.

carriers.label: Carriers
carriers.intro: How mechs get to the fight. Carriers began as converted amphibious ships, armoured trains, mining crawlers and cargo airships, and each bloc's carriers follow its geography. This tree runs past the present into Gen 3 and the war years, where the first warships built to fight in the atmosphere appear, and ends where the carriers of No Peace Past Luna begin. Dashed cards in the Gen 3 columns are projected; they haven't happened yet.
turns: A reactor is a battery charger
Merlins proved variable frames could land on a carrier deck. The Navy noticed that one carrier reactor could recharge a whole squadron's batteries at once.
Every bloc carries frames its own way
The United States goes by sea, the Pact by rail and ground-effect craft, and the League by mining crawler and old car ferry.
America's only helicarrier stays up nine hours on turbines. It's a carrier, not a warship, and it is never taken near a fight.
In orbit, carriers learn that frames win boarding actions but are too slow for open space, so they launch fighter craft beside them. Every carrier in 2327 still does.

Fusion and fission make lift cheap enough to armour. The Aerie and the Tsitadel are the first ships built to fight in the air instead of just carrying frames to it, and the last: the Lunar Mandate bans them.
fams: Flight decks that became swap pits.
From cargo airships to the first warships of the sky.
Tenders, catapult ships, and the way down.

nodes.t: Catapults, arresting wires and ninety jets
nodes.x: America's fleet carriers: nuclear-powered, catapult-launched, and built around Halcyon's Gyrfalcons. Their reactors turned out to matter more than their flight decks.

nodes.t: Variable frames on a carrier deck
nodes.x: Halcyon landed Merlins on a supercarrier to prove they could operate at sea. The real finding was below deck: one carrier reactor could recharge every battery spine in a squadron at once, where a shore base needed hours.

nodes.t: Supercarrier rebuilt as a floating swap pit
nodes.x: Kestrels don't need catapults; they need batteries. The United States rebuilt its supercarriers with swap bays where the catapults had been, charged straight off the reactor. One carrier can turn around forty Kestrels an hour without a single swap pit ashore.

After Svalbard the Kestrel carriers were refitted for Harriers and given point-defence lasers fed directly from the reactor, so they can fire for as long as the ship has steam. It's the best-defended swap pit in the world.

nodes.t: Beams reactor power to Harriers overhead
nodes.x: A Harrier carrier with a SKYLINE transmitter on its island, beaming reactor power to any Harrier in line of sight. It does what Ascension's relay does, without needing Ascension's permission. The Navy's carriers end up in orbit, but they keep the shape: the Ironshield of 2327 still has a supercarrier's flat deck and point defence fed straight off the reactor, and American doctrine still calls carriers flying citadels.

nodes.t: Well decks, tiltrotors and landing craft
nodes.x: Big-deck amphibious ships carrying marines, tiltrotors and landing craft, with a floodable well deck in the stern.

nodes.t: Garrisons standing in the well deck
nodes.x: Amphibious ships with raised hangars and a rebuilt well deck so Garrisons could stand upright. A Garrison can't swim, so landing craft carried them ashore two at a time. Six frames per ship, and the crew slept in what had been the vehicle deck.

nodes.t: The first ship designed around mechs
nodes.x: Tall hangars, frame-sized lifts, and a well deck Teamsters can wade out of in four metres of water. It lands a full fire-team company with its Drover IIs, then stays offshore as their workshop.

nodes.t: Flat-deck ships Japan won't call carriers
nodes.x: Flat-deck “destroyers” that are carriers in all but name, kept small and defensive by law.

A helicopter destroyer refitted to carry Kizuna rescue frames to earthquake and tsunami zones. The Japanese public watched mechs walk off a ship on live television and start digging people out of rubble.
A fast landing ship for Japan's outlying islands, with a stern ramp and a frame deck. It put the Hayates into the surf at Yonaguni during the Yaeyama Incidents.

nodes.t: Union amphibious ships for the Mediterranean
nodes.x: Union member navies' helicopter carriers and dock ships, built for evacuations and peacekeeping around the Mediterranean.

nodes.t: Fast ship for a modular task group
nodes.x: A fast roll-on, roll-off hull carrying three lances and every hardpoint module they might need. Crews refit the frames during the crossing, so the task group arrives already set up for its mission. Union carriers still work this way in 2327: the Luftkogge runs a multinational task group from its bridge, and the MRD's Vanguard refits its fighters between missions.

nodes.t: Icebreaker hull for the Arctic lances
nodes.x: Built for the Arctic seabed dispute: an icebreaker hull, heated hangars, and a reformer plant that refuels BZ-6 stacks from the ship's own diesel. It carried the lance that fought at Svalbard.

nodes.t: A Polar Carrier frozen in for the refugees
nodes.x: Projected. When the Canadian Front breaks, one Polar Carrier's Canadian crew take refugees north instead of home, and let the ice close around the hull in a fjord on Ellesmere Island. The reformer plant and heated hangars built to keep a lance warm keep a town alive through the winters, on whatever diesel they can find. The survivors call the ship the Hearth. When their descendants go out into the dark, they name their carriers after it.
nodes.z: Frozen in · its people carry the name into the dark

nodes.t: Bow-ramp ships for the Caspian and Pacific coasts
nodes.x: Pact landing ships: bow ramps, short range, built in numbers.

nodes.t: Tieniu over the beach in Azerbaijan
nodes.x: Landing ships with reinforced decks for kneeling Tieniu, used to put frames on the Caspian coast during the crisis. A Tieniu lying on a ramp can't fire back, and Merlins took advantage.
nodes.z: 2174 · the Pact moves frames by rail and ground-effect instead

nodes.x: Civilian roll-on, roll-off ferries and container ships. Every navy quietly counted them as reserve sealift.

nodes.t: Old car ferries with frames on the car decks
nodes.x: League states bought retired vehicle ferries and carry frames along the Red Sea and Gulf coasts in them, lying down on the car decks. Cheap, deniable and unarmoured.

nodes.t: A container ship that is secretly a mech base
nodes.x: Grey Lantern's floating base looks like any container ship in any port. Some of its containers are workshops, some are hangars, and two open into a launch rail for Lantern Customs. It's registered under a different flag every year.
A Eurasian tradition that never died: armoured trains guarding borders across distances no road network covers.

Tieniu walk slowly and break down often, so the Pact moved them by rail. Kneeling on braced flatcars, they could fire their shoulder cannons straight off the train. Their timetables came from a Tianlong logistics program called Tianshu, the first time the Pact let software decide where its frames went.

nodes.t: Trains that feed the fortress belt
nodes.x: A railway running behind the fortress belt that carries Tieshans, Tiebis and ammunition to whichever sector is under attack. The belt works because the trains move reserves faster than an enemy can walk. Tianshu writes the timetables, and reroutes them faster than any staff officer could.
Wide-gauge trains bringing Kalibr-305s, Iskras, MTU-7s and Tsars up to the border. It is the train in the Siege Question's satellite photos, with a 50 m shape under the tarpaulins.

A crawler the size of a city block, with a Pamir reactor, two Iskra turrets and a hangar of Mamonts. It has never moved more than a kilometre under its own power, and every bloc's satellites watch it try.

nodes.t: The first that can cross a border
nodes.x: A working Krepost, built for Moscow's push west into Europe: slow, close to unstoppable, and able to run its Iskras continuously off the reactor. It can't cross a river until engineers build it a bridge, and that's how its enemies know where it's going.

nodes.t: Where the Grafted Battalions were kept alive
nodes.x: Projected. On the North African Front the Safinas stop carrying Haboobs and start carrying the wounded. Their water plants and refineries are turned over to culture vats, and the grafts grown from the stolen cultures are fitted in their hangars, well behind the line. Each crawler becomes a sealed little world that keeps its people alive on its own water and its own tissue, and so does every ship Umoja builds after them. The Commonwealth keeps the name Safina for its carriers, and doesn't talk about what the crawlers grew.

nodes.t: Beijing's trains on lines Moscow never mapped
nodes.x: Projected. When the Pact splits, the Fortress Belt Railway turns to face west. Steppe outriders guide the trains along lines Moscow's planners never mapped, Tianshu reroutes them faster than the siege trains can follow, and Tieshan companies arrive at fights the Russians thought were days away. Beijing never stops building on the idea. In 2327 the line across Mongolia is the Ground to Orbit Accelerator, still run by Steppe crews, and it launches straight to orbit.
Open-cast mining machines weighing thousands of tonnes, crawling a few hundred metres an hour. The largest land machines ever built.

nodes.t: Mining rigs as mobile frame depots
nodes.x: League mining companies parked old crawlers in the desert as workshops for militia frames. The Type-01Q's recoil dampers came out of them.

nodes.t: A mining crawler that carries a battalion
nodes.x: Qadira rebuilt a bucket-wheel crawler as a mobile base, with a hangar for eight Haboobs, a workshop, a water plant and a small refinery. It moves at 3 km/h and hides inside sandstorms. These are the League's capital ships.
Huge, slow tracked platforms that carried rockets to the pad, and later carried cargo to the elevator anchors.

nodes.t: A swap point that drives itself
nodes.x: Bulwarks spend their lives seizing swap points, so the Army built one that brings itself: a launch-crawler chassis with Pitwagon bays, a turbine plant, and a Bulwark platoon riding on the roof. It's slow and impossible to hide, so it moves at night.
Helium hybrid airships that hauled mining gear to places with no roads. Slow and huge, they could set down on any flat ground.

nodes.t: An airship hangar for four Kestrels
nodes.x: America's first airborne carrier: a hybrid airship with a hangar gondola, swap bays, and turbine-driven fans to hold station. Kestrels launch by dropping out of the hangar and transforming. It's far too slow to survive anti-air fire, so it only works over the sea and empty desert.

Four ducted lift fans, turbines that burn fuel at a rate the Navy won't publish, and nine hours aloft. It carries eight Harriers and swaps their packs in the air. It's a carrier, not a warship: lightly armed and never taken within range of a fight. Only one exists.
The Rookery refitted with a dorsal rectenna to run its lift fans on SKYLINE power. Under the relay it has stayed up for thirty hours. Outside the beam it has forty minutes, which sounds familiar.

Production helicarriers on HT-20 turbine-capacitor plants, topped up by SKYLINE wherever the relay reaches. Still carriers, not warships: any commander who takes one within range of a Mamont is relieved of command.

nodes.t: The first warship built to fight in the air
nodes.x: A Rookery-class hull with an orbital warship's armour and catapults, lifted and powered by a fusion plant small enough to fly. The United States has never said where it got the reactor. It doesn't stay out of the fight: it carries a mass driver and laser batteries, and launches frames straight off its catapults.
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.t: Surplus cargo airships moving Gen 1 frames
nodes.x: League militias bought second-hand cargo airships to move frames across deserts with no roads. It worked until someone fired at one.
nodes.z: 2176 · too easy to shoot down in the Convoy Raids

nodes.t: Radar balloons over bases and borders
nodes.x: Tethered balloons that lift radars and radio relays high above bases, for far less than any aircraft costs.
Wing-in-ground-effect giants that fly a few metres above the Caspian at 500 km/h. Too strange to be ships and too low to be aircraft.
A ground-effect craft with a nose door and a reinforced deck for two kneeling Tieniu. In the Caspian Crisis it landed frames on beaches in hours, where the landing ships needed days.

nodes.t: Ground-effect carrier for a Tieshan company
nodes.x: Bigger, faster, and armed with rocket racks. A Kaspiy-II can land a Tieshan company on any shore of an inland sea within the hour. It can't climb, so it can't cross land.

A Kaspiy hull with a Pamir reactor driving its fans. With unlimited power it can climb out of ground effect for minutes at a time, the first Pact craft to fly with frames aboard instead of skimming. Every bloc worries about what happens if one comes down over a city.

Kaspiy-Atom lift under a Krepost's armour and Iskra turrets. It flies low and slow, it's very hard to bring down, and it carries a full breakthrough group of Mamonts. If one is ever shot down, a reactor comes down with it.
nodes.z: War's end · the Lunar Mandate bans reactor-lifted ships from Earth's sky

nodes.x: The Amaterasu reactor was too big for any normal frame, so Japan built a ship around one. The Hakobune is officially an unarmed disaster-response ship, with a hospital deck, lift fans and eight rescue frames. Its hangar is also exactly the right size for Takemikazuchi. Its first flight is what convinced the other blocs that fusion could fly.

nodes.t: The Ark goes north to Vladivostok
nodes.x: Projected. When Japan falls into China's sphere, the Hakobune's crew fly it north before Beijing can claim it, with Mitsurugi engineers packed into the hospital deck, and set it down at the company's Vladivostok subsidiary. Moscow wants the reactor. The Nashik pilots want the ship, and under their Oath it stays what it was built to be: unarmed, and sent wherever people need digging out. The Mandate grounds it with every other reactor-lifted ship, so after the war it goes up instead, with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles, to Europa and Io. The Ashva Compact's Sentinel-class carriers are built around its hangar.

nodes.t: Tugs and supply craft at the elevators
nodes.x: Small orbital tugs that moved cargo between the elevator tops and the early stations.

nodes.t: Tugs that carry Lifters to the job
nodes.x: Tenders with open cradles for Lifter frames, taking work crews out to new station segments. In the Rivet Strike they became the workers' fleet.
Larger tenders that take Rigger crews out for weeks on salvage contracts, with a winch bay and crew quarters. The Tether Incident was fought from two of them.
The first dedicated warships, with a mass driver along the spine and catapults for Marlinspike frames. Nobody has fought with them yet.

nodes.t: Carries frames down, can't climb back
nodes.x: A warship that carries frames down through re-entry and releases them in the upper atmosphere. It can't return to orbit on its own. Its armour and catapults are the template every atmospheric warship copies.

nodes.t: Frames for boarding, fighter craft for the long reach
nodes.x: By the war's last years every orbital fleet has learned that frames win boarding actions and close fights around stations, but are too slow for open space. The lunar yards' answer launches both: Marlinspike descendants off the catapults, and small fighter craft from a second deck. Every carrier in 2327 still does, and counts both as its fighters. After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building it for the UN, and UNEL's Safeguard is its direct heir. No other power will build in a slipway the UN controls, so within a generation each has yards of its own, and carriers of its own: the Ironshield, the Longchao, the Luftkogge and the rest.

fleets.label: Space Fleets
fleets.intro: The navies of the space age, from the first warships of 2186 to the fleets of No Peace Past Luna in 2327. Every class in the No Peace Past Luna faction briefs appears in the last two columns: the older hulls still in service come from the late era, and the newest classes from 2327 itself. Where a brief gives game stats, the card shows them: C for combat, F for fighters (frames and fighter craft together) and T for troops. The generations in between are the ones the briefs only hint at, dead ends included, and everything after the first column is projected. The war-era orbital carriers also stay on the Carriers tab.
turns: Warships before anyone can use them
The lunar yard builds catapult cruisers for every bloc. Nobody has fought ship to ship yet.
A single British dreadnought breaks the Russian inner fleet. Every navy spends the next century building dreadnoughts of its own.
Every power builds its own yards
The Lunar Mandate keeps Luna's slipways for the UN, so the powers build yards in their own orbits, and their ships stop looking alike.
Colonies start out with their sponsors' old hulls: American ships on northern Mars, Union ships in the south, Chinese ships in the Belt. Their own designs replace them one class at a time.
fams: Frames and fighter craft, launched together.

nodes.t: Armed tenders from the Rivet Strike
nodes.x: The station militias never fully disarmed after the Rivet Strike. Their tugs and tenders, with cutting gear and rivet guns bolted on, are the nearest thing to an escort in orbit.

A very fast corvette with two light coilguns and missile rails, at its best in wolf packs: screening convoys, marking targets and chasing raiders. Latin-heritage crews paint their hulls, pick dramatic call-signs and fly riskier than they should. Colony One still runs a few as heritage pieces.

One of the classes Colony One's remnant builds in hidden docks beyond the main lanes. None has been deployed openly: if the United States thought the colony had rebuilt a navy, it would come to finish the job.

nodes.t: Escorts paid for by the megacorporations
nodes.x: The American corporations that kept the war effort supplied buy escorts of their own to guard their shipping. They want hulls that are cheap to run and easy to trust, which is still what the Ballista is.

Three or four medium coilguns, a point-defence grid, and very little that breaks. Corporate fleets ran them through the war because they were cheap to keep, and they are still easy to maintain and easy to trust, if not as tough as Chinese or Union frigates.
The Constitutionalists' picket: American-derived, contractor-built, and wired to fight alongside US forces rather than alone.

nodes.t: Raiders under a new flag every voyage
nodes.x: Grey Lantern sells the war a navy of privateers: fast, disguised raiders that hunt anyone's freighters for anyone's fee. Their tricks outlive the company. False transponders, hidden guns and ships that look like something else turn up in half the navies of 2327.

nodes.t: Reactor-fed lasers on a picket hull
nodes.x: The Navy tries pickets armed only with the reactor-fed lasers that once guarded its Harrier carriers. In vacuum they shed heat so slowly that they can fire for minutes, not hours.
nodes.z: Retired · once coilguns got cheap, nobody wanted a ship that had to wait to cool

nodes.x: A modernised American hull for local defence and showing the flag. Like the rest of the Constitutional fleet, it can't be sent to war without Washington's approval.

nodes.t: The Ballista's replacement, built for brickwork repairs
nodes.x: Thick, patchwork-friendly armour and three or four medium coilguns, built for the fast, ugly fixes Martian yards are good at. Martian crews love them; Earth engineers would have a heart attack. The remnant still builds them in secret.
The Steppe crews who guided Beijing's trains in the Pact Civil War go up through the Ground to Orbit Accelerator. Their light, fast craft scout ahead of China's expeditions into the Belt.

Light and very fast, with agile vectoring for swarming. It is weaker than American or Union corvettes, but better at not being hit. Many have been sold into the Belt, where they serve as couriers and are slowly being replaced by Skyblades.

nodes.t: The backbone of the caravan escorts
nodes.x: Two coilguns and a modular rack on a very fast, nimble hull, kept polished like a racehorse. Skyblades guard convoys, hunt pirates and are replacing the Belt's old Steppewinds.

nodes.t: The Belt houses arm their tenders
nodes.x: The Belt's prospecting families bolt guns onto their tenders to stop claim-jumpers, then build faster hulls for nothing else. Every Skyblade crew can name the cutter its house started with.

nodes.t: The most dangerous frigate in the system
nodes.x: Four or five medium coilguns, two micro-fighters or drones, and the speed to flank, strike and leave. Steppe crews treat them like living horses. The Belt caravans prize the ones they can buy.

nodes.t: Built to treaty, crewed by many nations
nodes.x: The refounded Union builds escorts that comply with every treaty it signs: low emissions, careful fire control and room for inspectors.

Low-emission and careful, with excellent sensor discipline. Fluyts are built to avoid trouble rather than start it. The MRD inherited some and keeps them for courier work until its own corvettes are ready.

Four medium coilguns and very good navigation. Not as deadly as a Windchaser, but steadier and more fuel-efficient. The MRD uses inherited Caravelas to fill out its screens until there are enough Redlines.

The Directorate's own frigate: fast, cold-running, and built around predictive fire control that improves the longer it watches a target. Its captains tend to come from orbital mechanics and prefer simulated duels to live drills.

nodes.t: Armed tugs on the Orbital Front
nodes.x: In the war every fleet needs ships cheaper than a cruiser to watch the lanes, chase raiders and screen convoys. The lunar yards build armed pickets by the hundred, and most escort classes still in service in 2327 descend from them.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' pickets, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the lunar crews' pickets become the UN's patrol fleet. They enforce exclusion zones and escort relief convoys between Earth and Luna.
The backbone of UNEL's patrols, built to intercept unsafe traffic and stop other people's fights from spreading. Its crews come mostly from civil-service families.
Three precision coilguns, ablative plating and a thermal damping suite for working in lunar shadow. Arbiters are built to end fights, not chase them.
A fast escort for relief convoys and evacuation lanes, named, like the Tunis Works frames, for a desert wind.

nodes.t: Patrol frigate with a hospital bay
nodes.x: Guards shipping lanes and outlying settlements, and carries a hospital bay most navies would give to a transport.
Fast and lightly armed, sent ahead of every Ascendancy formation.

nodes.t: The first ships built for Jupiter
nodes.x: The Nashik exiles' first warships at Europa and Io are cutters armoured against Jupiter's radiation more than against weapons. They pull crews out of failing habitats far more often than they fight.
Escorts convoys along the Ascendancy's extraction routes and hunts the raiders who prey on them.
A small, self-repairing picket that guards Umoja's habitats and seed shipments. Its hull composites heal the way its crews do.
Umoja's patrol frigate, with sealed life-support and quarantine bays. Its first job is keeping anything alive and uninvited away from Ganymede.

nodes.t: Route patrol, named for the sworn pilots
nodes.x: Armoured for radiation and debris, and sent to anyone in trouble on the Jovian routes. The class takes its name from the Nashik pilots' oath name for themselves.
A heavy frigate for convoy defence and route control, with the endurance to stay on station through Jupiter's radiation.
A cold-running courier that carries messages and pilgrims between the Communion's scattered habitats without being seen.
A sparse, cold-hardened frigate built for very long voyages far from any dock. Pilgrims rarely gather in numbers, and when they do, it seems to have been arranged.

nodes.t: Cargo between the elevator tops, the Moon and Mars
nodes.x: Ascension's freighters move cargo from the elevator tops to the stations and the Moon. One of them carried Colony One's settlers to Mars.

nodes.t: Keeping the Moon and Mars supplied
nodes.x: Through the war the lunar crews keep freighters running to Luna and to a colony on Mars that Earth has stopped paying attention to. Colony One grows up on what they bring.
Found everywhere from Luna to the Belt, with deeply modular cargo, troop and science bays. Its name is a corruption of leyenda. Colony One fits its Veyendas out as homes.
The Constitutionalists' transport, built and serviced by the American contractors who run most of their logistics.

nodes.t: The ships that put Colony One on Mars
nodes.x: Ascension's landers set Colony One down in the north, and an unannounced camp in Melas Chasma months later. Colony One's own transports are still built around their life support.

nodes.t: The mother ship of Colony One's fleet
nodes.x: Long-duration life support and sealed biosystems tuned to Martian physiology, for moving troops and habitats and evacuating the wounded. Crews paint settlement murals on its walls.
Automated haulers bring Belt ice and ore inward on routes Tianshu plans years ahead. Their crews are few and their holds are huge, and when one wears out, someone always buys the hull.

nodes.t: “Black Star”: the backbone of Chinese logistics
nodes.x: Highly automated cargo and troop handling lets it run on a reduced crew. In the Belt it is the most common bulk hauler, carrying ore, migrants and whole clans in cramped quarters.
Built for habitability and crew welfare over capacity, and often carrying more inspectors than soldiers. The MRD uses inherited Fusiliers between its settlements.
A bulk transport for troops, colonists and their machines. It inherits the siege trains' job of moving a whole army at once.

nodes.t: Reconstruction cargo for a damaged Earth
nodes.x: The UN's first new hulls after the Mandate carry reconstruction cargo, refugees and relief down to Earth's orbit. Crews start calling them arks.

Carries troops, refugees, medical cargo or reconstruction modules, with the best environmental control in the system and almost no guns. Earth crews call Providences arks, after the relief ships before them.
Heavily armoured for radiation and debris, and built to get a whole habitat's people out when something breaks.
Named for the League convoys that kept the Jinn supplied. It moves water, feedstock, refugees and, when it has to, whole communities.
A transport that carries its own biosphere, so colonists, crops and livestock arrive alive across Jovian distances.

nodes.t: Anything that will fly, leaving Earth
nodes.x: After the war, people who no longer trust any government on Earth leave in whatever will reach orbit and keep them alive: old freighters, worn-out ice haulers, stripped transports. The descendants of the ice communities are among them.
Part transport and part settlement, able to survive for years with no outside support. What it carries is often holy as well as useful.

Ascension's lunar yard builds the first dedicated warships for every bloc: a mass driver along the spine and catapults for Marlinspike frames. Every carrier and battleship in this tree descends from them.

nodes.t: Frames for boarding, fighter craft for the long reach
nodes.x: In the war the lunar yards' carriers learn to launch both: frames for boarding actions and fights around stations, fighter craft for open space. Every carrier since counts both as its fighters.

nodes.t: The lunar crews' carriers, under the UN
nodes.x: After the Lunar Mandate the yards go on building the mixed-wing design for the UN alone, with interceptor bays and room for relief cargo.
Modular bays for interceptors, aid drones and research craft. Less armoured than an Ironshield but far more efficient, and crewed by lunar flyers proud of precise flying and minimal waste.

nodes.t: Frames down through re-entry, and no way back
nodes.x: Built to release frames in the upper atmosphere, and unable to climb back to orbit alone. Their armour and catapults are copied by every atmospheric warship.
nodes.z: War's end · the Mandate closes the lanes down to Earth

nodes.t: The Navy's flat deck goes to orbit
nodes.x: Barred from Earth's sky and unwilling to rent Luna's slipways, the United States builds its own yards and its own carriers, and builds them to look like the supercarriers they replace.

Built to survive everything except subtlety, with dense point defence and the largest fighter wing in the system. It deliberately echoes the old supercarriers: flat deck, rugged angles, industrial pride. Colony One keeps a few as deterrents.

An American-derived carrier with contractor-built support systems and command architecture for working alongside US forces. Built for deterrence and political signalling, not for a war it fights alone.
A carrier whose fighters fly on power beamed from orbital relays: the SKYLINE idea taken into space. It needs fewer fuel stores and far more trust in the relays.
nodes.z: Abandoned · a carrier that needs a relay can be switched off from somewhere else

nodes.t: Surplus war hulls refitted for Mars
nodes.x: Colony One's first carriers are worn-out war hulls the Americans no longer want, refitted at Phobos. They are too hungry for parts and crew to keep forever, and Colony One designs the Dustwing to replace them.

nodes.t: Half an Ironshield, built for Mars
nodes.x: A compact carrier with fewer crew, simpler repairs and room to double as a lab or a transport, built from Phobos Forgeworks frames. The remnant still builds them in secret. “We don't need to outgun Earth. We just need to outlast it.”
China's first carriers are built around Tianshu: fewer crew, more drones, and rotation control the American ships never match.
Less armoured than an Ironshield but more adaptable, with fourteen to sixteen fighters or strike drones and exceptional rotation control.

Beijing's first answer to fighter craft is a tender full of Tianshu-flown drones. The drones are good; the tenders are fragile. Their drone bays go into the Longchao, where strike drones still share the deck with piloted fighters.

nodes.t: Holds big enough to be hangars
nodes.x: Emptied, a Belt ore carrier's hold can take a squadron. Caravans carry their own fighters in them long before anyone calls the result a carrier.

Chinese carriers traded into the Belt in debt settlements become caravan flagships: mobile markets, arbitration courts and convoy commands. The houses care more about the hangar space than the fighters.

nodes.t: A home away from home for CPS pilots
nodes.x: Huge hangars and room for a large marine complement, paid for with armour. The Goldpurse lets its money do the talking. The Belt's prestige carriers are still Longchaos.
The refounded Union builds carriers to run multinational task groups, the way its Lance Transports once ran a lance. Each one carries a fleet staff before it carries fighters.
Reliable and sometimes over-engineered, with a strong defensive grid. Union doctrine treats it as a command centre first and a weapons platform second.
The MRD inherits Union carriers and spends decades learning what it would change: the hangars, the refit system and the command architecture.
Adaptive hangars reconfigure its fighters between missions, and layered energy shielding stands in for armour. Its decks feel halfway between a warship and a research lab.
The MRD's next carrier, still in prototype. The Directorate's remaining Luftkogges are to be phased out in its favour.
The Commonwealth's first carriers are bought from the lunar yards and refitted with hospital decks and water plants, like the Safina crawlers before them.

nodes.t: Named for the League's capital ships
nodes.x: Built like the mining crawlers it is named for, with hangars, workshops, a water plant and a hospital deck. Its fighters fly cover for evacuations as often as they fight.
Umoja's first carriers grow out of the Commonwealth's relief carriers and the grafting knowledge that went to Jupiter. Their hulls repair themselves.

nodes.t: A carrier that feels like an organism
nodes.x: Self-repair systems, biotech composites and sealed ecological architecture. Its doctrine is habitat defence, but its hangars hold units other powers find hard to look at.
Grounded by the Mandate, Moscow's fortress idea goes up: a carrier that keeps its fighters inside its armour.

nodes.t: A fortress that carries its fighters inside
nodes.x: Named for the legendary city that sank beneath a lake rather than be taken. Every crew member has an escape craft.
The Hakobune never flies in Earth's sky again after the Mandate, but it reaches Europa with the Nashik pilots and the Mitsurugi exiles. Its hangar is still the Compact's model for a carrier.
A carrier for rescue, convoy defence and habitat security, armoured for Jupiter's radiation. When one arrives, people believe someone might hold the line.
The ice communities' descendants leave in habitat-ships that carry everything they need, a long way from anyone else. Their first carriers are habitat-ships with hangars.

nodes.t: Named for the carrier frozen in at Ellesmere
nodes.x: A long-range habitat-carrier for the coldest places in the system. The Communion names it after the Polar Carrier that kept its ancestors alive.
The lunar yards stretch the catapult cruisers into line ships with heavier mass drivers, and sell them to every side in the war.
The first battleships from America's own yards: heavy coilguns, heavy armour and small troop decks.
Six to eight heavy coilguns, extreme durability, and a smaller troop deck than MRD or Union ships. Unofficial motto: “Steel over silicone. Fire over finesse.” Colony One uses its few as escorts.
A modernised American-derived battleship, built for deterrence and interoperability with US forces.
Built in the Black Docks and not yet shown in the open. If it ever is, the United States will know Colony One has rebuilt a navy.
Beijing's battleships trade weight of fire for Tianshu-coordinated precision and good frigate screens.

Six heavy coilguns and a precision-targeting suite. It hits softer than other battleships, so Chinese doctrine wins with AI-coordinated fire and better frigates. Wealthy Belt clans keep a few as prestige ships.

nodes.t: The CPS's first true capital ship
nodes.x: Strong enough to deter raids, cheap enough for a rich caravan, and modular enough to refit for trade war. Few caravans can afford one without great fortune.

nodes.t: Guns hidden in the cargo holds
nodes.x: Caravans tired of raiders fit heavy guns inside ordinary freighters and wait to be attacked. The Fortune's modular trade-war refits come from them.
Balanced line ships with strong mid-range firepower, built to fight as part of a fleet.
Thick forward plating and good endurance. Less punch than a Thunderbreak, but easier to keep running. The MRD uses inherited Galeóns for shows of force.

nodes.t: The most accurate battleship in the system
nodes.x: Built to set the geometry of a fight from stand-off range. Several Axioms can share targeting in real time. Its captains are austere and almost devout about optimal solutions.
The UN's battleships exist to anchor negotiations and declare jurisdiction, and are built to last rather than to trade blows.
Six heavy coilguns, very clean exhaust and systems built for long deployments. Its captains often come from diplomacy or civil government.
The Commonwealth's first battleships are built to hold a position while civilians get clear behind them.
Heavily armoured forward and built to hold a position while civilians get clear.
Umoja's capital ship, built to stand between its habitats and anything that threatens their ecology.
Moscow's lunar-built line ships hold the inner lanes until the Battle of Yernon, where a single British dreadnought breaks them. The Ascendancy builds every battleship since with that day in mind.
After Yernon, Moscow's planners build the biggest guns they can on hulls that barely move: siege monitors to hold the lanes.
nodes.z: Scrapped · they never caught anything that could run

nodes.t: Slow, and very hard to kill
nodes.x: Named for the warrior heroes of Russian epic. Heavily compartmented, with a way out from every station.

nodes.t: Named for the field of the great war
nodes.x: A heavily armoured battleship for decisive intervention on the Jovian routes, named for the battlefield of the Mahabharata.
Cold-hardened and long-ranged, and seldom seen. When Testaments do appear, it is usually by arrangement.
A British dreadnought arrives alone at the Battle of Yernon and breaks the Russian inner fleet. A Union written off since the European Front is a great power again, and every navy wants dreadnoughts.

nodes.t: The Senior Service has no rival in the void
nodes.x: Ten to twelve heavy guns, long-range precision cannon and a dense point-defence grid. The British kept the name to remind humanity who invented the concept. The MRD keeps its inherited Dreadnoughts indefinitely.

nodes.t: Sent only when protecting someone means facing a fleet
nodes.x: Named for the ancient capital of Kush, downriver from Khartoum. Few are built.
Within a decade of Yernon every navy has rushed out dreadnoughts of its own. The American ones are the biggest and the worst: heavy, unreliable and expensive to crew.
nodes.z: Scrapped · under UNEL arms reduction, which few navies minded by then

nodes.x: Eight to ten ultra-heavy coilguns and a spinal rail cannon. Less monstrous than Union or Chinese dreadnoughts, but more versatile. Every crew member must be unmodified. Colony One runs its few sparingly.
Ten to twelve ultra-heavy coilguns tuned with AI targeting harmonics. Its crews take cognitive optimisation to work with the targeting AI. Some have ended up in the Belt through debt settlements.

nodes.t: A bank vault and a courtroom
nodes.x: Built for long, lonely voyages as a trade-route anchor and neutral court. It has three bridges: one to fly the ship, one to count the money, and one to negotiate marriages.
The UN's first heavy ships are monitors parked over Luna's poles, watching the lanes from fixed stations. The Pillar is what they become once someone decides they should be able to move.
Hardened lunar composites, a spinal coil projector and the Custodian Array, a long-duration monitoring suite named for the lunar yard's giant. Its crews are almost monastic.
Named for Vishnu's discus. No single enemy ship is meant to break an Ascendancy fleet again.
Dense with self-repair systems and sealed ecological architecture. Few powers want to find out what its hangars hold.
Named for the Slavic thunder god, and built to hold the Jovian line when nothing smaller can.

orgs.label: Organisations
orgs.intro: The companies, laboratories and institutions behind everything else in the atlas, placed in the era where each first matters. Lines show what each grew out of, bought into or reacted against. Select one to see the machines, conflicts and doctrine it's tied to.
turns: Every mech maker began as something else: Halcyon built jets, Brannock-Hale tanks, Tianlong excavators, OKB-7 interceptors, Mitsurugi rescue robots. Their old products still show in every frame they build.
The Partnership Act let Brannock-Hale and Halcyon design, build, crew and maintain their own frames. It was meant to be temporary. Their lobbyists wrote most of its renewals.
Halden, Department Zero, Tsukuyomi Lab and Vireo all begin their work in the same decade, and none of them answers to a parliament.

An ethics panel that can stop a program, a lunar yard sworn to no bloc, keepers who won't command what they care for, a UN that has started bringing its own frames. The organisations that outlast the war are the ones that learned to say no.
fams: The US, Union and Canadian companies behind the West's frames.
State combines, design bureaus and Japan's capacitor maker.
From desert workshops to two design offices of Africa's own.
A consortium, its workers, and the houses beyond its reach.
Geneva's agencies, its borrowed white frames, and the institution the war forces on everyone.
Where the supers were made, and the bodies that answer for them.
Mercenaries, miners, and a canal that started opening containers.

nodes.x: America's fighter and ground-attack jet maker before mechs, and the source of every Halcyon frame's wing binders, avionics and flight-control software. It licensed Brannock's Garrison as the Sparrowhawk, then built the variable frames that defined US doctrine: the Merlin, the Kestrel and the Harrier. Since the Partnership Act it designs, builds, crews and maintains its own frames, and its engineers hold reserve commissions.

nodes.t: Tanks, construction walkers, then the Garrison
nodes.x: America's tank and heavy-equipment maker. It put a construction walker's legs under a tank's armour and built the first mech to see combat, the M4 Garrison, which nearly everyone has licensed, copied or rebuilt since. The Army's frames are Brannock's, from the Teamster to the Bulwark, and so is most of the Army's lobbying.

A European maker of armoured reconnaissance vehicles whose sensor masts and quiet running shaped every frame it built. It licence-built the Garrison as the Écuyer, then designed the standard-hardpoint Haubert that the Union's modular doctrine rests on.

nodes.t: Cold-weather frames from between the blocs
nodes.x: Canada's maker of snow tractors and ice-road haulers, then of frames: first licensed Garrisons built in Calgary, then its own Arctic designs on US chassis with Union sensors. It sells to Norway as readily as to Ottawa, and builds on both sides of a line nobody has drawn yet.

nodes.t: Brannock-Hale and Halcyon, chartered by Congress
nodes.x: The joint venture Congress chartered to do what neither company could alone: build the Concord. It took the first full-scale HT-20 plant, Bulwark armour and Harrier avionics to 40 m. About a dozen Concords later, some of its parts have left its depots on paperwork nobody can trace.

An Italian atelier that builds a handful of frames a year on Vauclair-Ehrlich bones, each for one named ace: the Falco, the Saetta, and now Roland, the only super the ethics panel has approved. Its racing stacks run at 140% of rated output, and its paint is always red and gold. It opened a workshop beside the Tunis line and built the Ghibli there.

The Monterrey Accords' industrial half: a Brannock-Hale line building Teamsters in Monterrey with Mexican crews. When Mexico joins the United States in the war, it becomes one of the country's largest frame plants overnight.

Projected. When Canada splits, Boreal splits with it: the Calgary plant builds for the United States and the Montreal plant for the Union, and the two companies trade patents through lawyers in Iceland. Each built half of the Aurora, and neither can build the whole.

nodes.t: Excavators, tractors, then the most-built mech in the world
nodes.x: Beijing's state machinery combine. Its excavators and tractors gave the Tieniu its drive train, and its factories built the Tieshan in thousands and now the Jingwei in series. It runs the frame trains and, through its orbital subsidiary, the prospecting tenders. It also built the network that now plans its wars.

nodes.t: A fighter bureau that builds heavy frames
nodes.x: A Moscow design bureau that built interceptors and bombers before mechs, and carried their heavy, aggressive engineering into the Medved, the Mamont and the Tsar. It opened a second line at Nashik, builds the Staya's wolves, and houses a department that officially does not exist.

nodes.t: Rescuers first, then the world's capacitors
nodes.x: Japan's disaster-robotics and industrial-capacitor maker. Its capacitor cores are inside nearly every linear and energy weapon in the world, and licensing them to everyone is Japan's real defence doctrine.

nodes.t: A rail scheduler that learned to plan wars
nodes.x: Tianlong's logistics program for the frame trains, and the first time the Pact let software decide where its frames went. It grew into the planner behind the Fortress Belt, cued the Air Umbrella, and under Order 21 drafts every operational plan for officers to approve. In 2184 it named Moscow as the second front.

The price of the Delhi Accession: an OKB-7 factory at Nashik building Medveds under Russian supervision, with engineers who rebuilt the cooling twice before Moscow agreed it needed rebuilding. Its first clean-sheet design, the Ashvin, is built around the Nashik Oath.

Registered quietly after Pact customs began holding Japanese capacitor shipments. On paper they are sales offices. In practice Mitsurugi has copied its design archives to both, and their staff lists are mostly engineers.

nodes.t: Engineers who left before the factory was taken
nodes.x: Projected. When Japan falls into China's sphere, the subsidiaries take engineers, archives and actuator lines out with them. The Ohio half is absorbed into American industry. The Vladivostok half goes a long way further, and its actuators end up in the Ashva Compact.
Shipyards and rail works that built ferries, rolling stock and tractors under French and Italian licence for most of a century, and kept the old Carthaginian habit of trading with everyone.
